SPECIAL TRADES INTELLIGENCE.

THE NEW POLITICAL ALLIANCE.
•TUE formation of a new Liberal party in the
present situation of our political affairs, how-
ever desirable, is still difficult. The Liberal
party is broken. Its ranks are full of con-
' fusion, and it has no recognised flag around
..which to rally its members. Luckily the
Tories have no policy beyond that of "sew-
age," hinted at by Mr. DISRAELI. There is
time; therefore, for the Liberals, if they use it,
to lay down a programme for the future, and
bring back discipline to their scattered forces.
At the present moment there are larger num-
bers than ever of Liberal men in England, but
they want two or three great questions upon
which they can be brought to unite. And in
the absence of suoh questions they have
grouped themselves in small parties round
subordinate proposals, and. on these they
expend zeal and resources which if more fitly
employed could not fail to produce most im-
portant national results. _ _

It may be said, too, that the great body of
the working men who have so recently been
admitted to our political struggles as
a constitutional force, have not as yet
been fitted into their right place in
the great Liberal army. They have special
questions which our old chiefs have only
partially accepted, and, so far as they have
thrown themselves heartily into the conflict,
they excite almost as much fear in their friends
as in their enemies. As a whole, however,
they hang on the skirts of the camp waiting
for terms which the old leaders have not the
courage to arrange and negotiate. Whoever
can adjust proper conditions of agreement
between the Masses of the working people
and the old Liberal party, will perform a very
necessary and very important work; and, in
this sense, great credit is due to Mr. MORLEY
for the attempt he made the other day at
Cannon-street. It was quite worthy his
intelligent zeal, as a friend of sound political
progress; and the causes of failure, should the
attempt fail, as we honestly believe it will, will
rest with those who gathered round him, not
with himself. The blunders which they com-
mitted no man singly could have prevented,
as the moderation and good sense of the indi-
vidual man has seldom much chance of success
in a crowd who personally, or, in principle, have
no common ground of agreement upon which
they can become reconciled for the purpose of
common action.

Addressing the great body of the working
men, we may say that they should either make
their minds up to take action, independent of
all Other Glat3A4o and parties, and carry on Eu 4

with points of difference enough to frighten
the most ardent controversialist?

The five financial propositions may be passed
over. The smallness of their number in some
measure compensates for their power of dis-
integration. But as agreement on financial
questions was always a party impossibility, it
would be unjust to blame the framers of this
programme for their mischievous potentcy in
connexion with party combination; as they
stand here they simply increase the difficulty
of forming the intended now party, and that
of itself is all that need ba said about them.

Liberal men who desire to see necessary
reforms in the State carried out will look at
this programme with chagrin and disappoint-
ment. Something more practical was naturally
expected from working men, or rather
,from
those who have undertaken to think and speak
for them. The common duties of the work-
shop teach our operatives that things require
to be done in their proper order, and to have
their parts adjusted in a fitting manner. Un-
scientific lumping will not produce a desirable
result. Hap-hazard is as much out of place
in the work of reform as it is in the making of a
shoe or a steam-engine, and if this be not
borne in mind we have nothing to expect but
bungling and disappointment. A great
political party by its agitation cultivates
public opinion, but its main object should, be
to concentrate and direct public action.
Sectional organizations spread ideas. General
organizations force legislation. In the new
body about to be called into life, we want a
power by which the coming election and the
new Parliament it will call into life may bo
made subservient to a safe and healthy pro-
gress especially in the interest of labour.
The practical questions therefore which it
raises should be few, but important ; whilst
those who lead in their advocacy should be
men known to ,the British public by their
experience, practical ability, and personal
influence. A blundering attempt to form a
groat party just now will be injurious in many
ways. It will throw the working men loose
from their allegiance to the party to which
they naturally belong, and it will encourage
the Conservative leaders to bid for their
support by every means in their power. And
though the thoughtful portion of the work-
ing people know where their true duty
lies there are multitudes of our work-
ing men, just like the weak and foolish
of all other classes, whose opinions lie
loosely upon them, and who, under the excite-
ment of political strife,. may be led into all
sorts of dirty byeways without having
.any
adequate sense of the degrading mess they get
into. Sober, thoughtful, correct action is,
therefore, what we need above all things at
the present moment. No impossible combina-
tions, no stupid futilities, by which friends
are discouraged and enemies brought into
aotisn with a promptitude and energy that
never could have come to them by the inspi-
ration of their own genius. It is not a
difficult thing to see that, should the Conser-
vatives slip into power through present lack
of discipline in the Liberal, ranks, they will
have a long lease of office if they are not to
be disloged until the Liberals can unite on the
three voluminous schedules of the Cannon-
street programme.

Besides if any political ps.rty accepted this
long catalogue of claims; it is difficult to seo
how they could go to work on it. No rallying
cry could,be got out of it. No party watch-

PRICE ONE PENNY.

word would answer where a dozen would be
necessary. No parliamentary candidate could
be examined on a political, social, and financial
creed, which no true believer could pretend to
understand. A "people's charter" with 29
points would break down and disqualify any
man who was not an utter glutton at
swallowing pledges. How could the public
help being blinded and confused by such a
fluttering of ideas, each made lively and
importunate by devoted adherents. A long
bill of fare may be a good thing,
but to be compelled to partake of all
the articles set down at one meal would not be
good. The millenium also is desirable, but it
cannot be reached at a bound, as the well-doing
that brings it must be progressive. •
It may be added also that the men who
undertook to promulgate the various points
contained in this new platform would require
half a life - time to prepare for their
work. They would require the read-
ing of MAGLIABECCUI, the eloquence of
BURKE, the omnivorous appetite of MACAULAY
for political investigation and disquisition,
rounded off by the impudence of CAGLIOSTRO.
There may be mep. in Englandlit to undertake
such a work of propagation, but at present
they are not known. We cannot for one
• moment persuade ourselves that the working
men of England will accept swell a platform,
because we believe they are in earnest, and
mean that the work of political, social, and
financial reform should be carried forward in
reality. They will insist on two or three
-questions which they can comprehend, and in
which they can feel a living intsirest. The
Land question, now connected with the eel-
cultural labourers' movement; the Edueatioa
question, now, through the state of things in
Ireland, coming on us as a life :and death
puzzle, two or three root questions which,
when settled, will put to rest a multi-
tude of minor questions growing out
of them. These are what the nation
wants and. must have. A platform bristling
with 29 points is one for talkers, not for men
who mean work, for men who find platform
gabble pleasant, not for those who hit from
the shoulder, and by decisive action make
victory secure. Our working men will only
sanction demands obtainable in the near
future. Measures to be carried—not ideas to
be discussed. If they pledge themselves it
will be to a policy which includes their special
questions as workers, and which, at the same
time, will enable them to throw in their
strength effectively for the welfare of other
classes, and generally for the furtherance of a
sound, practical, and progressive policy. -

LLOYD JONES.

MR. THOMAS BRASSEY, M.P. ON
WORK AND WAGES.

ONE of the most important contributions
to the labour question which has appeared ia
recent times has just been published by Mr.
THOMAS BIiASSEY. Workmen and their ad-
visers have not had a more instructive book
of facts presented to them than is comprised
in this record of the business of one of the
largest employers in the world. Mr. THOMAS'
BEASSET has long been known to have taken
a thoroughly enlightened view of the claims
of labour, and has on more than one critical
occasion supported those claims with the
authority- of a prominent capitalist. He has
now, after some years of audy, collected in
one volume the vast experienee of his father's

firm in all parts of the world. There are
plenty of employers who tive a copious Supply
of vague generalities alS6nt.l ivorlemen, eSpe-
cially if they happen to fie in Parliament.
And there are not wanting those
,who, on
occasions, are quite ready to flatter them, or
to appear as their representatives. Mr.
BRA.sSEy belongs to neither of these. His
work is essentially that of an employer, look-
ing on business from the employer's point of
view. But, at the same time, it takes a
just view of the workmen's position, and
establishes, by overwhelming evidence, many
:claims for which be has long contended
,in vain. The book is not one of vague
rhetoric or economic dogmatism. It censists
entirely of facts and statistics, broadly selected
and carefully compared. It is, in fact, and it
is a thing net often to be be Met with, a per-
feetly honest disclosure of the employer's
experience. It *e.ighs that experience with a
fair hand ; and whilst it admits the claims of
the workmen, it frankly points out their impru-
&beet; and their blunders.
,On the whole, they
have not had a more Valuable Collection of
faCts, from which on the one hand to learn,
with whieh, On the other, to strengthen their
claims and prove their case.
,The first proposition in the book disposes of
e popular fallacy that" wages are unnaturally
forced up" by the action of trades unions.
Workmen have long been aware that the value
of their unions consists mainly in rendering
wages steady, in preventing spasdomie
alterations
.of trade wages, and in . se-
curing the legitimate rise of market
,rates. Wages in the long run 'depend,
as the, workmen know, on the balance
between demand and. supply. As „ti.DA,Di
SMITH, here quoted, says, "The demand
increases necessarily with the increase of the
revenue and stock of every country, and can-
not possibly increase. without it." When, as
at present,. wages submit to this general
.law, the shallow pretenders to economic
science
,see in it only the machinations
of the trades unions, or it may be of the inter-
national society. The hook before us disposes
of this wide-spread absurdity. Examples in
every branch of labour are accumulated where
the natural result of demand has raised wages
far beyond the wildest dreams of any unionist
in countries whore combination was never
heard of. It is a popular error that *ages
have been rising exceptionally in this country.
Mr. BIiAsSOC proves, on the other hand, that in
none of the great countries of Europe have
wages risen so little as in this country.' In
France, Belgium,. end Prussia wages have
risen within 15 year's 30 or 40 per cent. At
the famouseegine works at Cruzot, for instance,
'where 1.6,000 men are employed, wages 20
years ago were V; francs a day. None now
receive less than 5 francs. In the meantime
in, Ertg,land the rise has been trilling. At the
Canada works in Birkenhead wages cliff not
-rise more than 3 per cent. between 1854 and

There is nothing which we hear more often
asserted than the enormous rise in the wages
of Bkilleti labour, Now the elaborate tables
here given by Mr. BRASSEY prove to demon-
stration that up to the year 1869 wages had
not very muolt increased in this country for 15
or 20 years, At the Canada works 600 men
are employed, and their wages are given for
every year from 1854 to 1869 inclusive. What
is, the result of these 16 years? The fitters
liad gained Is. in 305., the turners 0, the
coppersmiths had lost 9d,, the grinders had
Just 45., the smiths Is., the boiler-smiths had
gained 25., the bricklayers 0, the saddlers 0,
the forget:nen had lost 45., the painters had
List ie., the moulders had lest 6d., the joiners
had gained 2e., and the boilermakers had
gained 6d. Thus, on the whole, the wages of
1869 were distinctly lower than those of 1854,
whilht, throughout the 16 years tbe rice had
never once exceeded 6 per cent. In the mean.
time the trade of the country had grewn from
£260,000,000 its if.in to £547,000,000 it)
1870 ; and the exports of iron and steel have
doubled themselves within seven Yea"'

On page t4o,we hove a very elaborate table
.or .v6rage wows paid to all classes of skilled
uorkmen in a large locomotive factory for the
years 19 end 1869. The result of 13 cliffs-
rut tr.t.desi in this periodof te years amounts

to a rise of exactly `2(l. in 288., being for 1859
275. 11d, as against 28s. id. for 1869.
Some time ago we Were leetnred every
morning on the wickedness of the Shipwrights'
Trade Union whiohi it was said, had,. driven
away the trade from England by 'Unnatural
exactions. Mr. Iliu.ssEY disposes of these
charges by quoting from offioial tables the
rates of wages in the Sheerness yard and at
the Millwall WorG. At Sheerness there was
no rise whatever between 1859 and 1869. At
Millwall the wages of 1869 were exactly what
they were in 1851, except that shipwrights had
lost Bs. out of 403., and during the four years
preceding they had lost, 45., the period when
these charges Were at their loWest.

Since 1869 it is true a rise of wages has
taken place in several trades, arid within the
last six months the unexampled demand for
labour has led to sudden and great increase in
one or two trades. These oases are not, how-
ever, at all likely to be permanent. Indeed,
speaking generally, the rise of wages has not
at all kept pace With the rise in ,prices. The
true cause for wonder is, not that wages have
risen so much, but that they have risen so
little. The real source of this is doubtless to
be found in the stagnant condition of the
agricultural labourers. In this country alone,
of all others, he has no personal interest what-
ever in the soil. And the helpless condition
in which he lives forms as it were a low-tide
mark for the whole mass of English workmen.
The next proposition is that high wages do
not necessarily imply dear goods. We often
hear that every rise in wages inevitably raises
prices to the same degree, and we are some-
times told that it is suicidal for workmen to
raise their wages, as they have to pay the in-
crease back again in living. The height of
absurdity was reached when we heard a fana-
tical economist implore bricklayers not to ask
for mine hours instead of ten, as they would
make houses so dear that they would have
none to live in. Now the book before us
establishes this important point, that the cost
of labour 'is not determined by the rate of
wages. This is proved by a multitude of
facts in all parts of the world. For instance,
on some particular drainage works in London
wages were raised from 6s. to 10s. a clay; yet
the work per cubic, yard was cheaper at the
increased rate than at the low rate of wages.
English navvies ,at ss. a day were found to be
cheaper than French navvies at 2t. 6d. a day.
It was found that a London bricklayer at
6s. 6d. a day laid more bricks by measurement
than two country bricklayers at 3s. 6d. a day.
In Russia the hours of work are seventy-five
per week, and the wages one-fourth of the
English. Yet, "the mowing of a quantity of
hay, which would best the English farmer half a,
copeck, would cost the Russian proprietor
three or four copecks." The wages paid in a
French shipbuilding yard are almost exactly
half of those paid in -England; yet a French
ship casts ten per cent. more than an English
built ship. The cost of labour in smelting iron
is twenty per cent. less in France than in
England; yet the cost of •the pig iron in
France is 20s.' or 30s.' per ton more in France
than in Cleveland. The average wages
for puddlers are 7s. 6d. per day in Staf-
fordshire, fis..4d.'iu France, 4s. 9d. in Belgium,
yet the average price of the bar iron was
'.t6 10s. per ton in England, £7 per ton in
Belgium, and £8 in France. On the other
had in the hardware trade of America, wages
are double those of England, yet they can
export their goods to countries where wages
are only a quarter of these rates; and though
raW material and wages are twice as dear in
the 'United States as in England, they can
export spaies, shovels, axes, Viols, and pumps
to England. In faet, what all this implies is,
that dear labour well-applied is far cheaper
than cheap labour ill-applied. Higher intelli-
gence, labour-saving appliances, new machi-
nery, and superior organization will more than
compensate for increased wages. The cost is
entirely a matter of skill, etonomy, and
science, and these are actually stimulated by
labour bell* very costly. The dearest and
most costly of all kinds of production is where
no wages are paid at all--viz., in slavery.
And high' wages are happily quite compatible
with cheap goods. So true is the claim of the
workman, that he has not had his fair share

of the immense saving effected by the increasd
use of machinery, and. the higher organization
of labour. i

But if .the rate of daily wages affords no
indication of the cost of work, -the hours of
labour are no criterion of the amount of work.
To the discussions of the day it is common to
assume that a reduction of hours frOm ten to
nine is exactly, equivalent to an increase of
cost by 10 per cent. The book before us dis-
poses of that fallacy. It proves, by a multi-
tude of instances, that employers have often
within limits reduced the hours of labour
without adding to the cost of production. Re-
cently MIL Douras, the great cotton-spinners
of Malhausen, reduced the hours of labour
from 12 to 11 per day without reducing wages.
At the end of a month they found that 5 per
cent. more work was done in 11 hours
than had been done in 12. Russian labourers
work 17 hours per day; yet it is calculated
that an English labourer will do the work of
two Russians in a day of 10 hours. On some
English railway work the double shift system
was introduced, giving 8 hours for the day's
work. It was found by calculation that the
8 hour men did more work in the day than
the 10 hour men. At Messrs. RilisOMEs
1,200 artizans are employed. On January
2nd of this year the hours of work was reduced
from 58i to M. It has been found that the
work now precluded has been increased 12 or
15 per cent. It is not, of course, denied that
unreasonable reduction of hours may involve
increased cost, and where the motive power is
steam, this is, to a great extent, the natural
result. Bat it can be shown that under
favourable conditions a reduction of hours is
not necessarily attended by a loss in produe-
tion. Increased diligence and zeal in the
workman, combining with more careful
economy of labour, may .usually be made to
compensate for the whole, or nearly all, the
loss of time. But for this end fresh spirit
must le put into the concern, both by em-
ployer and employed.
But the most remarkable proposal in this
volume is that for the introduction of the
double-shift system. Mr. BIUSSEY declares
himself in favour of the 8 hour day whenever
it can be made practicable. The difficulty is
this, and it forms a dilemma of over-
growing importance. The advance of science
gives a larger and larger part to machinery,
and mechanical appliances. It is only by the
greater recourse to this that wages can be
raised or hours reduced. But the increasing
costliness of this plant makes it more and
more an economic waste to keep it long idle.
Costly machinery, in fact, will not pay its
former outlay, if it is only to be used eight
hours out of the twenty-four. On the other
hand, as the workmen grow in intelligence and
rise in thesocialscale, they demand and require
more leisure and fewer hours of work. Hence
this dilemma arises. As machinery is in-
creased, it must be used more hours if it is to
pay. On the other hand, as the workmen get
more fit to use maohiney they require to work
fewer hours, if they are to improve. This
dilemma is one which the workmen perhaps
have not fully considered. It accounts for
much of the bitterness of the recent struggles
to reduce hours. There was some sense in the
groans of the Master Builder the other day,
who looked with horror on the prospect of his
costly plant standing still at four o'clock on a
summer afternoon. Mr. BRISsEY now throws
out a solution for this apparently hopeless
dilemma; one which it seems ought to satisfy
both sides. Be suggests that wherever
machinery is to play a large part, the double
shift system should be introduced. That is to
say that the' working day for the whole stock,
plant, and standing " works " should be
• increased to sixteen hours, and the workman's
day reduced to eight hours, two gangs succeeding
each other in each day. By this means the
work of the maohine would be increased 60
per cent; whilst the work of the man would
be reduced 20 per cent. The machine
would work for two-thirds of the day;
and the men only one-third. The eco-
nomy in machinery would be 60 per cent.,
and the increased production would be 60 per
cent. At the same time the workmen would
gain two clear days, without at all diminish-
ing produotion, or necessarily ffeg any

reduction of, wages. And double the number
of workmen iirould be called into demand.
The details of this would be easily arrangeb
without making either shift night work: The
16 hours of the mechanics would be obtained
from 5 a.m. to 9 p.m., or (allowing 1 hour's
rest) to 10 p.m Then the first set would
work from 5 a.m. to 1 p.m., and the second
from 1 p.m. to 9 p.m., or (allowing two
intervals of half an hour each) from 5 a.m.
till 1.30 p.m., and from 1.30 p.m. to 10 p.m.
There would be this further gain in the
system, that when men worked only eight
hours per day, and one set left off work at
1.30 p.m. and the other began at that hour,
both might take their dinners at home. This
would be a great economy to the workman,
who would save the cost of the tavern; and a
great economy to the employer, who would
save the waste of the midday hour to his
machinery and plant.
There are, no doubt, great diffioulties in the
way of this system. They are all =trained
and criticised by Mr. BPASsEr, who decides
that the system is practicable. It has often
been carried out successfully on railway and
other works. We know that large coalfields
in Yorkshire and elsewhere have long been
worked on this system, and almost all
snbterranean work is so exeouted. We
must also remember that printing and many
similar trades of the highest skill are now
carried nn on the plan. And that the whole
of the vast maritime service, as well as the
railway service of the world, is carried on
thus. What can be successfully accomplished
in the complex organization of a colliery, a
steamship, and a railway, can be also intro-
duced into a cotton-mill or a building-yard.
Of course it does not follow that industry is
yet ripe for the enormous revolution And
expansion which this suggestion involves.
Its success would very largely depend on the
degree in which workmen are able to make
eight hours work nearly as valuable as that of
ten hours. If they could do this the em-
ployer could afford again to raise wages out of
the immense saving by the increased profit on
the plant. The problem is simply this :—To
make 16 hours of human labour (say at 10s.)
by 16 hours of machine labour equallo 10
hours of human labour (say at 55.) by 10
hours of machine labour. It is obvious that
the solution of the question grows easier, as
machinery plays a larger part in industry,
and. as its use is more and more economised.

This solution of one of the great industrial
problems is now offered to the employers with
the recommendation of a firm who have per*
•baps the largest experience in the world. It is
seriously worth the consideration of the work-
men. It offers to them from economie grounds,the
realization of their ideal—the eight hours day
—without diminution of wages, or increase of
prices, but along with a vast increase of eon*
nomic production, and employment for double
the number of men. It is plain that great
difficulties will stand in the way; and the
scheme is only applicable to industry based
upon a great organization of machinery and
plant. But it is the natural solution of the
industrial dilemma. And it may well be
looked on as the most valuable suggestion
which has in recent times been offered tri-
wards the improvement of the condition of the
workman.

It is impossible on the present oceasion tO
go into all the points established in the work
before us. One of the most interesting is the
proof by abundant inst‘nees that the cry of
English manufacturers being driven out of the
market ia a complete fallacy. It is shown that
notwithstanding the high wages in England,
the skill and strength of the English work-
man, and the organizing enterprise of .the
English manufacturer are as prominent as
ever, and that the complaints of the capitalists
are usually the loudest in countries where
wages are lowest.

There are plenty of observations, suggeg'•
tions, and warnings of great value to the
workman' scattered throughout the book.
Tier° is a fact for our temperance friends :---
" On the Great Northern Railway there was a
celebrated gang of navvies, who did more vrork
in a day than any other gang on the line, arta
always left off work an hour or an hour attd a
half earlier than arty othir hien. - Frog
Right and Duty are like two palm trees,—unless they grow together they bear no fruit.

and thus lead public opinion in the way in
which they think it should go—a task, we
are disposed to think, beyond their strength;
or they should .work for general objects as a
Section of the great Liberal party—a powerful
and important section it is true—having
common interests and sympathies with others,
anti willing and ready to co-operate with'
them. In this way they would give strength
as well as gain it by helping the general work,
about whieh all are agreed, and drawing in
return from the general body support for the
special questions which concern them more
particularly as working men.
Instead of following a course so obviously
to their advantage, and so practical, if real
work has to be done, they have made
a political oils podrida by stewing up
together every thought, idea, %lit movement
possessing any claim on popular support, under
the expectation, most likely, that by uniting
these several sections a groat Liberal party
might be formed, forgetful that those numerous
propositions, or articles of faith, are more likely
to become grounds of difference than bonds of
union; that discord, not harmony, will be the
result, and that separation and antagonism,
not permanent union and, agreement, are the
natural fruits of a union so preposterously
fantastical. Those who know anything of
party combinations understand how strong the
attractions must be by whieh men are brought
into joint action; and they know also by
an experience they cannot disregard by what
minute, almost imperceptible, differences they
are driven apart from each other, and
rendered powerless for the accomplishment of
a common object.

A glance at the Cannon-street programme
must satisfy any thoughtful politician how
likely it is to produce divisions and hostilities.
How utterly impossible it will be to unite

INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION.

The General Council of the Workman's '
Peace Association has just issued their Second
Annual Report and Balance-sheet. The re-
port states that during the year sixty-five
public meetings have been held in favour of
International Arbitration, most of the meet-
ings having been held, in our largo towns;
and that, notwithstanding the Alabama diffi-
culty, several of these meetings have been
attended by such largo audiences, that many
persons were unable to gain admission, the
resolutions having been moved, and sup-
ported by men of all shades of political
opinion.
The members and friends of the association
have obtained 102,000 signatures to Parlia-
mentary petitions praying the Government to
take the initiative in establishing a permanent
system of International Arbitration, while
several organized bodies of working men, in-
cluding the Birmingham, Preston, Oldham,
Maidstone, and other Trades Councils the
Northumberland Miners' Association, and the
last Trades Union Congress which met at
Nottingham, have adopted similar petitions,
the total number of petitioners being nearly
600,000.
The report also congratulates the members
on the publication of the " Arbitrater," a
journal established and conducted by members
of the Association. In addition to the General
and Executive Councils and staff in London,
the Association has, in the provinces, over one
hundred agents, committees and branches
engaged in the work of propaganda, a large
proportion of them being men holding positions
of influence and trust, to which they have been
elected by their fellow working men, which
positions give ;thorn great opportunities of
influencing their order in favour of Inter-
national Arbitration. The income for the
year has been £1,012 13s. id., while the
expenditure has been £l,OlO 11s. 101 d., thus
leaving a balance of £2 is. Std. At the
recently held annual meeting, Mr. Edmond
Beales was re-elected hon. president, Mr. B.
Lueraft as treasurer, and Mr. W. it. Cromer
as secretary.

STOCKPORT.
TRD LONDON JOINERS' STRIKE.

A large meeting of the joiners of Stockport was
held on Monday at the Golden Ball, Mill!gate, to
receive a report from Messrs. Bonny and Burgess,
a deputation from London now visiting the pro-
vinces on behalf of the London strike.
Mr. Roberts having been called to the chair,
briefly related the circumstances under which the
meeting had been called. Mr. Benny then entered
into a lengthy explanation of the origin, progress,
and present position of the strike, which had now
continued for nine weeks without the slightest
signs of weakness on the part of the great bulk of
the men. The support which they had rceived from
the different towns in Lancashire was very en-
couraging and had greatly stimulated the London
men to remain firm in their demands.

Mr. Burgess then gave a retrospect of the nine
hours movement, showing how it had originated in
London, from a conviction on the part of the
workmen that they would never enjoy the long
promised blessings pt machinery until they ob-
tained a reduction of the hours of labour. After
along and severe struggle in 1859, we accepted a
drawn battle. At that time they were lectured
and preached against by men who ought to have
known better. The great question of a reduction
of the hours of labour had made such pro-
gress that some sixty towns in the provinces
were now enjoying the privilege which the men
of London found it so difficult to obtain. Ile an-
imadverted on the ill-omen for the future which
presented itself in the great difficulty which
skilled workmen found in obtaining their reason-
able demands. One would think from what had
taken place that we were attempting some dia-
bolical outrage on the property of our employers.
A whole industry had been stopped, and large
masses of men had to undergo great privations,
and for what ? To obtain the common necessa-
ries of life, and maintain a decent position in
society, they asked a reduction of 51. hours, and a
rise in wages of 7d. per week, also a codo of
working rules, which meant nothing more than a
common-sense agreement between workmen and
employers, by which labour should be bought and
sold. These things they were determined, with
the assistance of the provinces, to obtain.

Aftf,r some discusziion a resolution was unani-
mously passed to levy the trade in Stockport 6d.
per week in support of the London men.
With the appointment of a committee and some
routine business, the mooting separated, after the
usual vote of thanks to the chairman.

MANCHESTER.
TUB STOItEMABONS.

The masons in Manchester have been agitating
for a considerable time to commence work at seven
o'clock in the morning, and an advance of wages
from 'lid. to Bd. per hour. Last Tuesday they
gave notice that if the demand was not conceded
they would strike on Thursday morning, giving
two days' notice. A conference took place between
the operatives and Mr. ilinchcliffe, Mr. Marshall,

and Mr. Johnson on the part of the employers on
Wednesday afternoon, and, after a lengthy discus-
sion, it was agreed that on the Ist of March,
1873, work should commence at seven o'clock in
the morning, working 491 hours per week, and
the wages to he advanced from 71d. to Bd. per
hour.

such a demand. He trusted those present knew
the nature of the work uport which they were
entering, that they were in earnest, and deter-
mined to work together.

Three resolutions were then proposed by the
secretary and agreed to unanimously, which de-
clared, in effect, the meeting was of opinion that
nine hours should be the working day, or fifty-
four hours per week, and that this time should be
so arranged as to allow the workmen to leave at
one o'clock on Saturdays; that wages should be
increased to 7d. per hour, and that certain regula-
tions should be enforced with respect to extra pay-
ment for overtime.

Mr. Mitchelley and Mr. Davis, both members of
the General Union of London, aldressed the
meeting at considerable length, and were received
with much enthusiasm.

Ultimately a resolution was moved by Mr.
ililton, seconded by Mr. hart, and unanimously
agreed to :

That this meeting agrees with the course taken
by the trade in convening a meeting, and pledges
itself to send delegates from the various shops and
jobs to a committee meeting to ho held at the
Charleville Arms, Glo'ster-road, on Friday, the
16th inst., to carry the agitation to a successful
issue. The present committoo is also empowered
to draw up a circular and send to the joiners' trade
of Brighton.
Cordial votes of thanks to the delegates from
London and the chairman, brought the proceedings
to a close.

articles.title: LIVERPOOL.
articles.text:
LIVERPOOL.

TILE HOUSE rAINTERS.

At a meeting of the Liverpool operative
house painters, on Wednesday evening, the 7th
inst., it was unanimously resolved to memorialise
the masters for an advance of Id. per hour on
their present rate of wages, six months' notice to
be given from the Ist October next. It was
further resolved to memorialise the employers to
adopt the nine hours system. During the meeting
a resolution was passed suggesting that all painters
Who (lid not belong to either of the existing
societies should immediately enrol themselves as
momber3.

BIRMINGHAM.
GENERAL GUN TRADE ASSOCIATION.

The first meeting of the General Gun Trade
Association was held on Tuesday evening, at the
Town Hall, Birmingham, for the purpose of pre-
senting a balance-shoot to the members, and
placing the society upon a firm basis. Mr, D.
Kirkwood, the president, occupied the chair, and
there was a fair attendance.

In opening the proceedings the Chairman said
they had met for a special work of great import-
ance. It was intended to submit to the members
the first efforts of the General Gun Trade Asso-
ciation, anti, in doing so, the committee believed
they were bringing before them that which would
materially tend to increase the welfare cut inte-
rests and also add to the power of the Association.
(Applause.)
Mr. Monk (the secretary) then read the balance-
sheet, which showed the following results :—Re-
ceipts, £lO7 33. 4ti. ; expenses, £3O Is. lid. ;
balance, £7B 7s. Lill Of this amount £7O was
invested by trustees in the Birmingham Joint
Stock Bank, and the remainder was in the hands
of the treasurers. Attached to the report was
an aildress, which, after pointing out the difficulties
of the movement, concluded as follows :

It has been the fashion among interested and
selfish men to decry trade societies as monopolies
and unjust restrictions, and for no other reason
than because they take measures to prevent the
supply of labour exceeding the demand, and by
making restrictions to prevent men finding their
way into a trade who have not earned the right by
a period of probationary servitude evils which, if
allowed to remain unchecked, reduces the skilled
workman to the condition of the unskilled la-
bourer, mid bequeaths pauperism and want as the
row ard of a life-time of honest and industrious
toil. The promoters of this Association believe
that the seeds of combination have fallen at last
upon favourable ground, and that a powerful and
prosperous trade association will reward their pre-
sent efforts. We ask the members of the gun
trade, one and all, to become recruit§ in the great
army of inclnstrial and social regeneration—to
have faith in the principles of union, and rely
upon it, wo shall scion learn to look upon this
society as the best safeguard of our interests, the
only means by which the artistic and mechanical
skill of the workmen engaged in the gun trade can
be acknowledged and remunerated as they de-
serve.

Tho Chairman moved tho adoption of the
balance-aheet.

Mr. Pinder (vice-president) seconded the
motion.

AUG. 17, 1872._

Mr. Brown (a delegate from DLulaston) sup-
ported the motion.
The motion was unanimously adopted.
Mr. Monk then read the rules of the Associa-
tion, which were adopted.

NOTTINGHAM.
BUILDING TR.IDES COUNCIL.

The above council held its second meeting on
Tuesday at the Old Angel Inn, Stoney-street.
The object of the council is to amalgamate the
various societies in the trade, and to work for the
general welfare of all. Hitherto the societies
have been, in a sense, working contrary to each
other's interests, because of one society asking for
an advance of wages or a reduction in the hours of
labour at one time, and another at another time,
and so on. When parties were driven to strike
considerable injury was being done to others who
bad no concern in the affair. This council will
endeavour, as far as possible, to obviate all such
difficulties, and to establish a more harmonious
and consistent mode of " action " in the trade.
The building trade of this town comprises twelve
societies, the great majority of which have given
in their adhesion to the council, and it is hoped
that in a short time the whole of the societies will
be united in this council.

articles.title: MISCELLANEOUS TRADES NEWS.
articles.text:
MISCELLANEOUS TRADES NEWS.

LONDON.—A mass meeting of the dustmen,
slopmen, and scavengers of Paddington and Bays-
water, was held in the Duke of York, near
Paddington•green, for the purpose of considering
the expediency of memorialising the contractors
for an advance of wages; also to reduce the hours
of labour from 16 to 12. A resolution to the latter
effect was put by the chairman, Mr. Collins, and
carried unanimously.
PorrEniEs.—lt is probable that there will be a
serious conflict between the chinamakers and their
men in the Staffordshire Potteries. Hitherto it
has been the practice to pay on all work that
stands the test of the Oven, but there is a move-

suspended.
PRESTON.—On Saturday the printers of Preston

CHATTIAM.—The dockyard labourers at Chatham

the Loris of the Admiralty for the extra shilling

of pay fur those labourers who even now receive
but the inadequate sum of 15s. a week.

articles.title: LONDON CARP ENTERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON CARP ENTERS.

The dead lock that characterised the position of
the strike during the past week continues in respect
to both masters and men. Efforts, however, will,
it is understood, be made to bring about fresh
negociations. The code of working rules de-
manded by the central committee has been more
or less the rook upon which all previous negocia-
tions; were wrecked, and means will be devised
to meet the difficulty, if both parties are not too
obstinate in their own right or admission or rejec-
tion of these points.

However unpalatable another resort to arbitra-
tion might be, there would be nothing in it
dishonourable, either as regards the men or the
masters.

Since our last the following is a report of the
proceedings :
The weekly delegate meeting of the carpenters
took place on Thursday night at the Brown Bear.
Mr. Davis was voted to the chair.

Letters were read from Messrs. Binney and
Burgess, the deputation at present organizing in
the provinces.
A letter was read from the Macelesileld Arms
district, asking the committee to place the strike
men and lock-out men on the same weekly
dividend. A large mass of correspondence was
gone over having relation to tho withdrawal of
men in various firms, and of the conduct of the
masters in procuring hands through agents in
country districts.
The report of Messrs. Sadler and Wright giving
an account of their progress in Yorkshire, included
an application for hands to be sent down to
that district, where work was to be had for a
number of carpenters.

I Mr. Smith proposed a resolution to the follow-
ing effect :
That the carpenters, in view of tho action of the
masters, are prepared to maintain the terms of
their memorial, though they are still open to
negociate upon the questions in_dispute.
Mr. Sinclair followed in support of the proposi-
tion.

The resolution, after a lengthy discussion on the
part of several delegates, was put to a vote and
carried unanimously-.
Mr. Harris made a proposition that other lead-
ing firms should he struck against in addition to
those already closed, selecting those who are the
most busy.

Mr. Westcott seconded the proposition. Ito
believed by acting thus !natters would soon be
brought to an issue..

Mr. Mortimer spoke against the proposition,
thinking it was an unadvisablo step to take at the
present moment.
The resolution to strike against other firms was
negatived.
A proposition was made that the non-society
married men, with families, should receive an in-
crease in their dividend. It was finally agreed
that the scale of the dividend should remain un-
changed in respect to all parties.

After the transaction of some routine and formal
business the:meeting adjourned.

The masters' committee state positively that
they have no present intention of meeting again
before September, and that, with a few exceptions,
the whole of the firms struck against have a suffi-
cient number of men at work to enable them, with
but little inconvenience, to execute all the
contracts they have in hand. They also
state, however, that they are prepared at a
fsw days' notice to receive any deputation
from the carpenters who may wish to see them,
upon a request to that effect being officially sent to
their secretary, Mr. Bird, always providing that
such deputation is etnpowered toiffect a settlement
of all the questions in dispute—viz., the hours,
the wages, and the code of working rules. With
respect to the hours, they are:prepared to consider
the re-arrangement of hours agreed upon with the
rnasons, providing the carpenters can advance any
solid reasons why these hours would not suit the
requirement of their trade; as to the wages, they
are not prepared to make any further advance
than that already made to the masons—from SI to
By. per hour; and as to a code of working rules
--considered of such importance by the men—
they are prepared to discuss such a code, and that
any difference of opinion arising thereon should
be referred to arbitration. This may be taken as
the ultimatum of the masters. It therefore
remains to be seen whether the central committee
will be prepared to recommend the delegates to
re-open negociations with the Masters' Committee
and send a deputation, with full powers to treat for
a settlement upon the above basis. Under the
circumstances; this would undoubtedly be a wise
and proper course for the committee to take, and
for the delegates to act upon, as being the only
available means of bringing about a settlement.

The central committee paid their weekly

dividend on Monday, at the rate of us. 6d. per
man, with 14s. 6d. to the men on strike from the
firm of Messrs. Brass's and Jackson and Shaw's,
being an advance of 6d. upon the dividend last
week. The numbers of men receiving the dividend
was 1,600. The committee continue to receive
very favourable reports from their deputations in
Lancashire and Yorkshire.

The Central Committee of the Carpenters sat in
deliberation for some time on Wednesday upon the
policy to be pursued in the present crisis; and,
although no final decision was arrived at, it may
be taken for granted, from the feeling that gene-
rally prevailed, a resolution will be proposed to the
delegates at their meeting on Thursday night
recommending the opening of negotiations, and
that they appoint a deputation to meet the
Masters' Committee at die earliest possible time,
with full powers to treat for an immediate settle-
ment of all the points in dispute. It was also
quite certain that such a recommendation will
meet with strong opposition from the "no sur-
render" party among the delegates, but hopes are
entertained that the majority of those present will
"look at facts as they are, and not as they wish
them to be," and approve the appointment of the
deputation. In that case the deputation will pro-
bably consist of five in number, who will receive
their instructions from the Central Committee.
The committee had also under consideration the
recalling of the deputation now in the country,
but this question was deterred pending the vote of
Thursday evening. The committee had also
before it the copy of a circular issued by a large
building firm at Pimlico, who usually employ
about 100 first-class joiners, but who have now
about 50 men working in the shop, requesting the
indulgence of their customers for the delay in exe-
cuting their orders, and for the manner in which
the work was being done. Thrs circular was cited
as a proof of the inconvenience under which the
employers are suffering.

TIIIII2f3DA.Y.

At the meeting of delegates this evening,
a resolution in favour of sending a deputation to
the employers, with full power to effect a settle-
ment of the dispute, was carried by 9-1 votes
against 19.

articles.title: LONDON PAINTERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON PAINTERS.

A crowded meeting of the Painters and Decora-
tors delegates' was held on Monday night at the
Three Doves tavern, Berwick-street, Soho, for the
purpose of considering the case of Mr. Waller's
men, of whom a large number were present ; Mr.
G. Shipton occupied the chair. Ho stated that
every effort had been made to effect a settlement
of the points in dispute with Mr. Waller, but in
vain, and the committee, therefore, recommended
that the firm be at once struck for the full terms
of their memorial—viz., 51 hours, at 8!,-d. per
hour, with a code of working rules.
After some discussion the following resolution
was unanitnoully adopted
That as Messrs. Waller and Son, of Chelsea, have
violated the agreement mutually entered into be-
tween thorn and the house painters and decorators in
their employ, we consider that men cannot continuo
to work on that firm with honour to themselves or
proper observance of the general interest of their
fellow-workmen, and we therefore resolve to call
out the whole of the men, and pledge ourselves to
use every means in our power to support them so
long as may be necessary.
The Chairman stated it had been reported to the
committee that the men in Mr. Ilanting's firm
intended to strike. He did net know whether this
was so or not, but he would take this opportunity
of stating that any men who struck work without
having first received the sanction of the committee
and delegates would not reecive support from the
funds of the movement. After the trawaction of
some routine busine3s the meeting adjourned.
In accordance with the resolution unanimously
adopted on Friday night by the house decorators'
and painters' delegation, the whole of the men
employed by Messrs. Waller and Son, of Chelsea,
struck work at 12 o'clock on Saturday. These
men, about 100 in number, are all first-class
workmen, and have been employed for a long time
past at the numerous blocks of large mansions
erected on the estate of the Marquis of Westmin-
ster, in the district of Belgrave and Eaton squares.
On Monday a meeting of the painters on strike
from Messrs. Wailers', of Lyall-street, Chelsea,
W,IB held at the Phamix Tavern, for the purpose
of organizing the strike committee and passing
resolutions for the conduct of the strike.

Mr. Shipton said that one of the chief points
in the tactics they had now to pursue was not
only to keep the old hands from going back, but
now ones from going to take their places, unless
Messrs. Waller would give the terms asked.
Their first duty then would he to organize picket-
lug committees, to superintend the pickets to be

sent out. It would be the duty of the pickets to
attend all jobs that Messrs. Waller have in hand,
and inform any hands that might be at work, or
about to begin, of the terms on which the old
hands had come out. But in so doing they must
not ía any way infringe the criminal clauses of
the Trades Union Act by endeavouring to in-
timidate or coerce men in any way whatever.
Several other speakers then addressed the meeting,
and eventually picketing parties were appointed
and told off to visit the twenty different jobs
Messrs. Waller have in hand. The following
handbill was than distributed for circulation :
" Caution.—To the House Painters of London..
—All house painters are requested not to apply
for work at Waller and Son's, Lyall-street, Eaton-
square, until further notice, as all the men have
struck work in consequence of Mr. Waller having
violated his agreement with the men relative to
the terms on which they were to work.—By order
of the House Painters' Central Committee." It
was stated that three of Messrs. Waller's men
were remaining at work, and refused to come out.
In reference to one, it was stated that he was a
very old man, who had been with the firm a groat
number of years, and that if he left there the
probability was that he was too old to get work
anywhere else. He bed always been well con-
ducted. It was resolved :
That he be allowed to remain with the character
of an honourable man, and that he be not looked
upon as a black-leg, owing to his age.
It was further resolved :

That any man may obtain one week's work and
yet pot be struck off the strike pay, but that if
he obtained work at any place for over a fortnight
he be considered as having no further claim on
the strike fund.

On Tuesday another meeting of the painters on
strike from Messrs. Waller's, Chelsea, was held at
the Phomix Tavern. The chairman stated that
the pickets appointed on Monday had visited all
Messrs. Waller's jobs in the course of the after-
noon, and had reported that they had only found
five men at one job and two at another. Mr.
Waller has succeeded in getting twelve now men,
all of whom had gone into work. It was then
resolved that they he waited upon by the pickets,
and informed that it was a strike firm, and that
they were at work on strike jobs. It was reported
that 15 more of the old hands had obtained em-
ployment, making a total of 15 gone to work at
other firms out of the 80 men who came out.

articles.title: LONDON PLASTERERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON PLASTERERS.

The committee sitting at the Sutherland Arms,
St. Martin's-lane, *paid a dividend on Monday,
which, although not quite so largo as the usual
dividend of 65., was receh ed by the men without
dissatisfaction. There is groat difficulty on the
part of this branch in obtaining money in the
shape of levies from the men who are at work.
Levies have been made in the provinces, and the
money is coming in pretty regularly ; but the
London men do not seem to support their brethren
to' the extent that was expected. An appeal to
the bade has been issued, setting forth the urgent
wants of the committee, and unless the appeal is
responded to freely, there is every likehood that
the plasterers' dividend will be oven less next week
than this, in which case they will not be ablo to
hold out and continuo the organization for any
lengthened period.

articles.title: LONDON BRICKLAYERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON BRICKLAYERS.

The bricklayers era holding several district
meetings. Fourteen in number have already
been held, and several more are yet to take place.
Their committee paid on Wednesday us, dividend,
those on strike receiving 235. weekly. There are
not many of this branch of operatives on the
funds of the society, and the trade is becoming
more thoroughly organized than it has been
for many years.

articles.title: LONDON LABOURERS
articles.text:
THE LONDON LABOURERS

In addition to the twelve lodges they hava
organized, the labourers have established a new one
at Kensington, and on the 19th another will be
formed in the Holborn district. The men intend
to hold a public meeting next Tuesday evening to
explain the object of the society and to enrol
members.

The labourers who struck work on Wednesday
afternoon at Messrs. Jackson and Shaw's job, the
new Colonial Offices, in consequence of Mr.
Browning, the bead foreman, discharging the de-
putation of labourers who waited upon him with
the object of obtaining an advance in their wages
from 3td. to 51d. per hour, have visited the other
jobs of the firm, including Burlington-house,
Piccadilly, and the Midland Railway Rotel,

.Euston-road, and also the yard of the firm at
Pimlico, and, it is stated by their delegate, suc-
ceeded in "drawing out" nearly the whole of the
labourers at those places, with a pledge that they
would not resume work until the members of the
deputation were reinstated in their situations.
The steam cranes at the above works are also at a
standstill, as the drivers and !stokers who work
them are treated and paid as labourers, and turned
out with the other men.

The labourers on strike are no less deserving of
favourable consideration, as the action they took
was grounded upon a natural but unfortunate Mis-
apprehension. In the reports of the masters'
meeting of the 31st of July it was announced, by
mistake, that the labourers had been placed upon
an equal footing with the mechanics so far as
wages were concerned, whereas they were only
to receive a farthing instead of a halfpenny. They
sent a deputation to Jackson and Shaw's manager
to represent what they had read, and, instead of
replying that the statement was premature, be
summarily discharged them from their work, and
GO of their fellows struck to have them reinstated
without first consulting Messrs. Kenny and Hal-
loran, their representatives on the Atnalgamattd
Building Trades Committee, who would have ad.
vised them rather to communicate the facts in
writing to the head of the firm. However, that
has since been dono, and, as the mentleave the
wages part of the question for final adjustment
when the time for a general settlement has arrived,
their best wishers are not without hope of seeing
them all speedily reinstated.

articles.title: AMALGAMATED BUILDING
articles.text:
THE AMALGAMATED BUILDING

TRADES COMMITTEE.

A meeting of the Joint Committee was held on
Tuesday night at the Three Doves, Castle-street.
The brieklayers, plasterers, painters, metal workers,
and labourers wete represented by their several
delegates. A long discussion took place on the
position of the building dispute and the best way
of obtaining a settlement with the masters. The
following resolution was passcd

That the delegates of this amalgamated com-
mittee resolve to take the opinions of the bodies
they represent as to the propriety of appointing a
deputation to elect the masters to treat for an
mediate settlement of all points in dispute.

articles.title: LONDON SHOEMAKERS,
articles.text:
THE LONDON SHOEMAKERS,

A meeting of the Somers-town section of the
Heavy Branch of the Metropolitan Boot and Shoe
Trade was held in the Queen's Arms, Euston-
road, on Tuesday night—Mr. Bingham in the
chthr—for the purpose of considering 'the expedi-
ency of adopting a general uniform rise on tha
present standard of wages, or of memorialising.
the cnployers for an advance at the rate of la par
cent. The Chairman, in his remarks, said ha
totally deprecated the notion of a strike. Tho
masters would long since have granted an advanee
had they been properly applied to. It was re-
solved unanimously to memorialise for the advance
of 10 per cent., subject to the decision t.) be ar-
rived at at the next mass meeting. •

articles.title: LONDON BAKERS,
articles.text:
THE LONDON BAKERS,

The position of affairs between the master
bilkers of London and the journeymen anel
operatives has now assumed a very serious aspee%
and it is not at all improbable that, if the negetiu.
tions now pending do not run as smoothly as
could be wished, before many weeks have elapsed.
the bakers of London will have followed tho
example set by the builders. At the meeting hela
last weck at the Duchess of York it was 6ot forth
in a roport received from the Central Board of the
London Union that a suggestion had been made
that 12 journeymen and 12 master bakers should
meet on an open and public platform in conference,
then to discuss and, if possible, settle amicably thu.
matters now agitating the trade.
In accordance with that suggestion, a deputation
from the Trade Council of Operative Bakers has
just waited upon the Master Bakers' Trade Pro-
tection Society.
Mr. E. Adams, as spokesman, said they wore a
deputation from the Council of Journeymen, sent
o ,ti,ratdtseeerrtrlotitnectwiuhrietcheormiintittreveascoluls:inblle oottlillaetmtliliel
conference upon the various quesCons now
agitating the trade.
Mr. Dwarber, the chairman of the committee,
said, in answer, it had long been the wish of the
committee to meet the •operatives in conference,
but no steps had been taken on account of the dis-
union of the Men. Now that the dolegatis could
speak in the name of the whole body of the
men there should be no delay on tho part of
the committee to bring it about as soon as

the men were ready with their points for dis-

mission.

_
Mr. Clarke moved, end Mr. Gibbons seconded
(both masters)
That this committee is prepared to hold a con-
ference with delegates appointed by the London
Trades Council of Operatives upon the various
questions affecting the relation of the trade so soon
as the journeymen are ready with their platform.
This resolution was carried, and the deputation
withdrew.

A meeting of the delegates of the journeymen
was alsoheld, at which it was determined, for the
better carrying out of the objects of the Unions,,
to amalgate the two Unions which existed hitherto
under the names of the London Union and the
Amalgamated Union. A long debate also ensued
upon the "platform principles," the hours of com-
mencing work being the chief point. It, how-
ever, was unanimously agreed to that four o'clock
should be the time. The remainder of. the
principles have not yet been decided upon.
On Saturday evening a mats meeting of the
journeymen and operatives was held at the Grey-
houikd Hotel, Old Kent-road. The chair was taken
by Mr. Peter Fink, who said that, with regard
to the time of work, he went to a dele-
gate meeting recently when all the delegates
brought up the reports from various parts of
London, and one and all were unanimous as to the
four o'clak time. Mr. Strickland, one of the
delegates appointed, who attended a large meeting
of delegates, reported the proceedings. The
unanimous conclusions arrived at were that the
men should make certain time from four to four;
that the masters should not employ any boy in the
bakehouse unless apprenticed; that for Sunday
work a master should pay a foreman 2s. Od. and a
Second hand Is. fid. extra. With regard to the
amount of rise of wages no definite decision could
be arrived at, so it was referred to a committee, as
the chairman stated.

A crowded special meeting of masters' was hold
at the Masons' Arms, Watney-street, Commercial-
road—Mr. Murray in the chair—to Consider the
practicability of an alteration of the working
hours, in order to meet the views of the journey-
men. BMW) considerahle dise.ussion took place,
and ultimately the following resolutions wore
adopted :
That any twelve hours would be satisfactory,
three batches with two men, four batches with
three men five batches with four men, to be com-
pleted in the time.
That foremen and single hands should be paid
is. 6d., and second bands is. extra for Sunday
bakings. That in the event of wages being
advanced, the allowance of bread should be taken
into consideration, with a view to its abolition.

On Tuesday night a meeting of journeymen
and operative bakers was held at the Royal
George, Westminster-bridge-road, "to take into
consideration thehest means for adopting the 12
hours movement and a rise in wages." The meet-
ing was convened by the committee of the 14th
branch of the London Union, and was presided
over by Mr. 3. B. Marley. There were also pre-
sent a large number of delegates from various
parts of London. -
The chairman, in opening the meeting, referred
to the proposition made recently that a conference
should be held between twelve journeymen and
twelve masters, and trusted it would be attended
with good results. At a recent meeting of the
Central Board of the London Union, it was re-
solved that there should be a general rise of 3s.
per week for every man, that they should not
commence befora 4 o'clock in the morning, and
that Sunday labour should be abolished. With
regard to the East-end bak-re, he had just heard
from the Secretary that on Monday their brethren
in that part of London had turned out, that 100 of
these had obtained their terms, and the remainder
had marched through the streets from two o'clock
until ten, and were making collections to defray
their expenses and to keep the men on strike. A
goodly sum had been realized front the master
.bakers, and he understood that if those who wore
now on strike did not obtain their terms', they
intended to stop out until the projected conference
with the Trades Council and the masters was
held.
Mr. Strickland stated that great efforts were
being made to bring about the projected confe-
rence as soon as possible, and it was generally
believed that an amicable understanding would
be arrived at. lie concluded by moving :
That this meeting fully approves the movement
now beine made by the operative and journeymen
bakers of London for the amelioration of their eon-
dition, and pledges itself to support the eame by
every means in its power.
This was seconded and carried.

On Wedneiday evening a erosvded meeting of
delegates from nearly every branch of the London
Trades' Council of Operative Bakers was held at
the Admiral Carter, Smithfield, to consider the
Tarious;:points tl be laidCdown:asia:rlatform of

principles to put before the master bakers at the
conference which is to be held between 12 master
bakers and 12 journeymen, to settle the differences
now existing in the trade. The chair VMS occu-
pied by Mr. George Howe, the President of the
Council, and there were also present representatives
from no less than 25 branches and several local
clubs. A discussion, which lasted for some hours,
ensiled, in which almost every representative took
part. The following principles were ultimately
agreed to as the basis of the demands of the men:
—l. That a working day shall consist of 12 hours ;
work not to commence before 4 in the morning. 2.
That Sunday bakings shall be abolished. 3. That
there shall be a universal rise of 3s. per week per
man. 4. That the "sack" money shall be con-
sidered the legitimate right of the operative. 5.
That overtime shall be paid for at the rate of Is.
per hour for foremen, 9d. per hour for second, and
6d. for all other hands. Another resolution was
also adopted, to the effect that the bakers of
London, seeing that the employers were the
medium between them and the public for supply-
ing them with funds, were willing to make a levy
upon their members for the purpose of assisting
them in stamping out the undersellers' shops.

articles.title: LONDON CABMEN.
articles.text:
THE LONDON CABMEN.

The cabmen employed by Mr. Mayhew, an
extensive cabowner, of Great Ormond-street, have
gone on strike. It appears that at the end of
last week three of their number were dismissed,
and as great dissatisfaction has existed amongst
the men for some time with regard to the pay-
ment for cabs and the hours of labour, the others
have turned out until these men have been rein-
stated. Mr. Mayhew employs 43 cabmen and
5 "odd" men. A considerable number of yard-
men or ostlers are by this strike also deprived of
work, and will suffor most, as, unlike the others,
they have no fund to fall back on.

articles.title: AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF
articles.text:
THE AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF

CARPENTERP.

Air. J. D. Prior, who has just been almost
unanimously re-elected as general secretary to the
Amalgamated Society of Carpenters, returns thanks
as follows in the present monthly report :
rsiLLow-Mnunints,--I beg to tender you my
sincere thanks for the expression of confidence
whieh is shown in the votes just retttrned.
During the past year I have endeavoured to
the best of my ability to attend with punctuality
to all communications, and to supply the branches
with their various requirements as speedily as
pBssible. When I entered on. the duties of my
office we possessed scarcely a book or document
at the General Office; the entire machinery for
carrying on the business of the society has since,
been provided; the confidence of tlie members,
which had received a severe shock during the
late disturbances in London, has been fully
restored; and serious difficulties, caused by the
determined opposition of the parties who have
been excluded from the society, have been success-
fully overcome. All this has caused a largo
amount of anxiety and extra labour, and at times
I have found it impossible to carry out the duties
of my office to my own satisfaction ; but the
gratifying mark of your approbation which I have
now received will stimulate me to energetically
renew my endeavours to discharge faithfully the
duties with which I have been entrusted, and to
make it my constant study to increase the useful-
ness and to extend the influence of our society.—
I am, faithfully your',
JOHN D. rItIOR.

articles.title: LONDON ANALGANATED SOCIETY OF JOINERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON ANALGANATED
SOCIETY OF JOINERS.

From the monthly report of the London Amal-
gamated Society of Carpenters and Joiners, now
being issued for the use of the members only, it
appears that the balance in hand in March last
was £1,709 Os. 91., and at the end of the June
quarter, up to which the accounts were audited,
the sum stood at £1,792 Os. 4d. The income
through twelve branches amounted to £220, and
the expendtiure for the same quarter was
£lOl 10s. 4id. There are very few men. belong-
ing to the London Amalgamated Society receiving

A proposition was laid heforo a meeting
