articles.title: GENERAL UNION OP CAR-
articles.text:
THE GENERAL UNION OP CAR-

PENTERS.

The last monthly report of the Operative
Carpentera and Joiners' General Union of Great
Britain and Ireland sums up its review of the
position of affairs thus :
The Amalgamated Building Trades Committee
are at a dead lock; but the deputations of the
Central Council of the carpenters and joiners are
systematically organizing the whole kingdom, and
funds are flowing in to such an extent that victory
may iafely be predicted. A general lock-out on
the part of the masters is not feared, but xather
minded, as it will test the earnestness of the men,
who appear now to be united to a man.
One part of this statement seemed to receive
confirriaation on Saturday, as the finance committee
at the Brown Bear, presided over by Mr. Thomas
Hall, tho treasurer (Amalgamated Union of Car-
penters and Joiners), and Mr. C. Matkin, the
seeretary (General Union of Carpenters and
Joiners), were in a position to state the dividend
this week would certainly not be less, but most
likely more than last week. According to the
same report, there are 66 towns, including Liver-
pool, Manchester, Leeds, Sheffield, ani Birming-
ham, where the employers and the men have
agreed upon a code of working rules, one of the
points for which the London men are now con-
tending. It also appears that last month, at
Chorley, an agreement was come to with the
masters to fix the week's working time at 49
hours, at 7d. an hour, with a code of working
rules, while at Keighley the working time was
reduced from 64 hourssto 601 at the same rate of
pay, with a code of rules, and on and after the Ist
' October next, a similar regulation is to come into
operation at Blackburn. Strikes are now on at
Sheffield and Leicester, towards which the General
Union has contributed, in the shape of strike pay,
£3BO. The General Union has seven branches in
London, and in the first week in July 63 members
were included in the present strike, in the second
64, in the third 49, and in the 'fourth 21, the
amount distributed amongst them for the four
weeks being £162, in addition to the dividend
from the Nine 'Hours Strike Fund.

articles.title: RAILWAY SERVANTS.
articles.text:
THE RAILWAY SERVANTS.

On Thursday week a meeting* of the men
employed by the Great Eastern Railway Company
was held in the Working Men's Hall, Stratford,
for the purpose of taking Melt'sures to obtain a
reduction in the hours of labour, and a rise of
wages averaging about Ss. per week over the
present settle. The chair was taken by Mr.
Baxter Langley, and there were about 600 men
present, including drivers, guards, signalmen,
stokers, porters, and every other grade. A
memorial setting forth the requirements of the
men was adopted, together with resolutions
pledging them to stand by it firmly.
A crowded meeting of persons employed by the
Great Western Railway and Metropolitan Rail-
way Companies was held on Wednesday week at
the Elephant and Castle, Harrow-road, for the
purpose of taking measures to obtain an increase
of the rate of wages and a reduction of the hours
of labour. The chair was taken by Mr. Chapman,
who briefly stated the object of the meeting. Mr.
Baxter Langley said that a rise in the price of
necessary commodities meant an actual reduction
in the value of their wages, and as there was at
the present time so much combination between
the Stock-Exchange dealers and sellers to raise
the prices of things necessary for living, so com-
bination among all grades of the working classes
was necessary to obtain a proportionate rise
in the price wherewith to purchase them. As an
instance, let theta take the present extraordinary
rise in the price of coals. It was not generally
known, but he could vouch for it as a fact, that
there was at the present time such a combination
among the coal proprietors and three of the
railway companies—namely, the Great Northern,
the Midland, and the London and North-Western
Railway Companies—to keep up the prices of coals
as was utterly without precedent. He had lately
been making inquiries as to who had profited by
this rise, and he had ascertained that there were
in this combination 28 coal-dealers on the Stock
Exchange and the three above-named companies,
together with several coal proprietors. The coals
which in 1869 were only 18s. 3,1. per ton were
. now in London charged &)s., and the reason put
forth for this extraordinary rise was the increased
wages paid. He had made inquiries as to what
extra wages was paid, and he found the working-

men had only got Is. 9d. per ton extra; and
while the monopolists only paid Is. 9d. mon for
the coal, they actually put 12s. per ton on the
price charged to the public-10s. 3a. difference
for themselves. He could tell them more, that
there was a contract between the parties that the
railway companies were not to carry coal ouly far
the 28 parties in London specified, and the coal-
dealers were not to supply any others only at
such fancy rate that they could not do anything to
reduce the present high rate. The meeting was
addressed by Messrs. Billing, Boom, and many
ethers, and several resolutions were passed with
great enthusiasm advJeating combination among
railway servants for the maintenance of their '
own interests.

The dirwtors of the Bristol and Exeter Rail-
way, in answer to an -application from the men
employed in the locomotive department for an
advance of wages, owing to the greatly increased,
prices of provisions, have granted an advance
of 2s. per week for all hands, together with rates
of overtime in proportion. A meeting of the
men was held the same evening, at which the
concession was acknowledged by unanimous votes
of thanks to the directors and Mr. Tames Pearson,
the superintendent.

The Amalgamated Societylof Railway
Servants
continues to make very rapid progress in all parts
of the kingdom. On Monday evening a great
meeting of railway men was held at Bristol, Mr.
George Chapman, the general secretary, in the
chair, and it was resolved to form a branch there.
Over two hundred men promised to become
members.- A. meeting of railway servants was
held at Righbridge on Sunday, under the
presidency of Mn. John Graham, the , organizing
secretary of the society, when about fifty in emb rs
were enrolled. A meeting was held at Gloucester
on the previous (I,ty, when 60 members joined the
branch established at that place. At Oxford, on
the same day, a meeting was held and a lodge
opened. Professor Rogers, of Oxford University,
addressed the gathering, urging all the men to
join the society, but on no account to 'Twit to
strikes when differences arose between themselves
and their employers. On Monday last the goo 3,
guards at Oxford petitioned their employers for a
reduction of their working hours to 10 per diem,
which was immediately granted. Several
branches have been opened at Manchester, and
nearly 4,000 have joined the Amalgamated
Society in that tqwn. Altogether about 20,090
men are now in the union.

articles.title: COAL MINERS.
articles.text:
THE COAL MINERS.

DMMONSTRATION AT FARNWORTII.

A. demonstration of miners belonging to the
Farnworth, Kearaley, and Worsley districts took
place at Farnborough on Saturdly afternoon.
The occasion was the anniversary of the formation
of the Amalgamated Association of Miners. There
were miners present from Rochdale, Bolton, Dean
Church, Little Lever, Bury, Radcliffe, Keanley,
Little Hylton, Worsley, and other districts.
Accompanied by bands of music they perambu-
lated the principal thoroughfares of Farnwortb,
after which an outdoor meeting was held in
field near St. Jchn's Church.

Mr. Handel Cossham, colliery proprietor,
Bristol, occupied the chair.

The meeting was addressed by Mr. T. Halliday,
president of the Amalgamated Association of
Miners; Mr. W. Brown, vice-president; Mr. IV'.
Pickard, miners' agent, Wigan; and others; and
the following resolutions were passed :-
1. That this meeting expresses its pleasure on
seeing that the wages of the miners and other
workmen connected with collieries in this and the`
surrounding districts have been advanced of WA
without having dlsturbed the relations between,
the employers and the employed or caused strike)
in the district; likewise expresses its pleasure is
seeing the eight hours per day system of work so
generally.adopted in the district, and believes that
the adoption of boards of conciliation and arbitra-
tion would be the best means of preserving the
good relations between capital and labour which
so happily now exist.
2. That this meeting desires to express ha
pleasure in seeing the Miles Regulation Bill
passed by the Houses of Parliament without its
being materially injured, and begs to 'thank Mr.
Bruce and the Government and those members of
Parliament who have assisted the Government ie.:
passing such a bill as appears to be satisfactory
and just to the public generally; and that
copy of this resolution be sent to Mr. Gladstone
and Mr. Bruce.
3. That this meeting considers the passing
the Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1871 a
piece of class legislation a n d such as reflects die'
credit on trade unions which they, in our opinion/
do not merit; end we express our determinatiot!
not to rest satisfied until the said Act is lepeal°4
or so modified as not to bear arbitrarily on tho
trade unions of this country. •
4. That this meetiug desires to press on the°
Government the propriety of preparing dalinkthor
recess such a masters' and servants' payment
wages bill bill as will make compulsory the payintgl
, of wages weekly without any deductions haviS

made therefrom whatsoever; also a bill for,
amending the law relating to compensation for
injuries done to workmen through the neglect of
persons appointed to manage works on behalf of
employers.
- • -
-

Rain fell heavily during the afternoon, which
marred the success of the meeting.

ADTANOB OF couazas' WAGEA.

The collier 4 of the Ashton-under-Lyne district,
which include(' Stalybridge, Dukinfleld, Hyde,
Haughton. Green, Denton, Hurst, and Park Bridge,
a fortnight ago sent a circular to the colliery pro-
prietors demanding an increase of 7i per cent. on
their present rate of pay, and also requesting that
wages be paid weekly instead of fortnightly, as
is now the ease. The men asked for an answer
to be returned on Saturday last, and, on that
evening a delegate meeting of the men was
held at the Manor House Inn, Ashton-under-
Lyne, for the purpose of receiving the replies.
The masters have consented to increase the
wages as requested, but refused to pay weekly.
The advance commenced on Tuesday. Within the
last six weeks the wages of the miners in the dis-
trict have been increased twice at the 'rate of 10
per cent. and now again 7i, making 27i per
cent.

A mass meeting of the miners of East Derby-
shire was held on Tuesday at Clay-cross. The

men resolved to form themselves into a union
to demand that their working hours be reduced
to eight per day.
At a demonstration of the minors of Cannock.
chase on Tuesday, at which the Rev. G. Pool,
vicar of Burntwood, presided, addresses were deli-
vered by Mr. W. Brown Horth, of Stafford, Mr.
T. Halliday, President of the Amalgamated Asso-
ciation of Miners, Mr. W. Pickard, Parliamentary
Agent, and others. Resolutions wore passed re-
cognising the adoption of the eight hours' system,
and the passing of the Mines Regulation Bill,
weekly wages, and the compensation of workmen
injured by employers' negligence. My. Cossbam
alluded to industrial partnerships as the only way
of settling the question between capital and
labour.

The strike amongst the bituminous coal colliers
in the Rhonda Valley and other portions of South
Wales has beeon brought to an end by the masters
conceding the demand of the men for an advance
of 4d. per ton. Two thousand men and boys
commenced work on Monday morning, after lay.
ing the pits idle for a fortnight. The masters have
been influenced in yielding by the fact that a
general advance of ten per cent. has been an-
nounced to take place throughout the district.

articles.title: MINERS IN THE OLDIZAII DISTRICT.
articles.text:
THE MINERS IN THE OLDIZAII DISTRICT.

A fortnight ago the colliers of the Oldham dis-
trict sent in,a notice to their employers asking for
an advance of 16 per cent., and threatening to
strike if the advance was not cOnceded within
fourteen days. The masters held a meeting on

Lain, on Wednesday morning, the offer of the

,-

That colliers' wages in the Wigan and West

resoived that circulars should be issued asking for
an advance of wages to the extent of 40 per cent.,

and to be given to all the men and boys employed

Ikumhers 10,000 members, while 1,445 joined
lately. On Monday the men at Xivetonvaric
colliery and at the aigh Boyd joined the aasoeia-
tioa, Aatong agitation is now going on at Clay.

cre-se and other places, for the purpose of forming
a union for Derbyshire. and Nottingham.
The North of England Iron and Coal Industrial
Company has conceded the recently-asked advance
of 21. per ton to the ironstone miners employed
at their South Belmont Mines, near Guisborough.

At a meeting of the ironstone mine owners of
the Clevel uld district, held in Middlesborough on
Tuesday afternoon to consider the request of the
miners for an advance of 2d. per ton, it was un-
animously resolved that, looking at the substuntial
advance granted to the ironstone miners, the
demand of a further advance contained in a circular
dated 3rd August could not be entartoined. A
lock-out is considered probable.

articles.title: AGRICULTURLL L &BOURERS.
articles.text:
THE AGRICULTURLL L &BOURERS.

,r SOXIMSET AND GLOUCESTER.

Meetaigs in favour of the Labourers' Union are
to be a 3 d on Friday evening, the 16th, at Illmin-
star, atd on Saturday' evening, the 17th, at Yeovil,
at which Mr. G. Mitchell (one from the plough),
Mr. Arch, Mr. Benjamin Taylor, High Bailiff of
Peterborough, Mr. J. Mitchell of Lyme, and
others will attend, and address the meeting.
We understand that especial reference will be
made to the late speech of the Bishop of Gloucester
and Bristol, in regard "to horseponds and
agitators" who, although having been called to
account, still maintains his opinions, as will be seen
from the following, written by him since our last
issue :

The Bishop of Gloucester has explained his views
on this subject in a letter to the secretary of a
local agricultural union. His conclusions are :-
1. That our Gloucestershire employers have, for
the most part, dealt fairly with their men hitherto,
and that now, in the altered state ot prices, they
are preparing to deal fairly, and to raise wages to
the point to which they ought to be raised. 2.
That it is wrong :and utterly unjustifiable for
strangers, who can know nothing of our local cir-
cumstances, to come among us and to stir up
dissension and to set class against class. 3. That
we ought not to send our Gloucestershire men
away from us to other counties, but study to make
them happy, and contented at home. This is the
substance of what I said, and of what, as at pre-
sent advised, I abide by. Of course I feel it
possible that I may be wrong to some extent as to
(1) ; but this I solemnly declare' that during the
nine years I have been in this diocese no oluses
have ever been mentioned to me of systematically
unfair wages in any parish that I have visited, and
I certainly have spoken freely with all classes, and
have made very free inquiries. I am of course
here alluding to past years. During the last two
years we have been passing into a new state of
things, and it is to this new state of things that
our attention has most seriously to be turned. I
have inquired anxiously, and I have certainly
arrived at the conviction that our Gloucestershire
employers are meeting fairly the altered State of
things. The general deign of my speech was to
encourage them to go onward, and to follow the
many good examples that are being set them
throughout the county. Englishmen may he led,
but will not be driven. The truest friends of the
labourer are not those who make the greatest pro-
fessions, but who humbly endeavour to do justice
to both sides.

articles.title: DORSET.
articles.text:
DORSET.

Stickland, near Blandford, is the head-quarters
of various other branches forming of the labourers'
unions in Dorsetshire. The Secretary, Mr. J. W.
Barnett, has, during the last two weeks, gone
round to visit the branches at Dorsetshire, Bad-
port, Yeovil, Sturminster-Nowton, Ibberton,
Whitechorch, Abbey-Milton, Chizzleborne, Piddle.
town, Affpuddle, Bore Regis, Afilborne St. Andrew,
Kingstone, and Blandford. Excepting four, these
are doing well, and hundreds are joining weelly.
Wages have risen in nearly every place visited.
The first quarterly meeting of the executive of
this eociety was hold at the central office,
Leamington, guMonday, when several members
of the consulting board attended. Mr. Joseph
Arch presided. The balance sheet showed that on
the current account, after the payment of all
expeuses, there was a balance in hand of £5O,
the weekly expenses being about £5O, chiefly in
the wages paid to the delegates engaged in
organizing "districts," and affiliating them with
the union in all parts of the country. Towards
this work funds are necessary until the roll of
membership is so extended as to render farther
organising unnecessary, and theu the society
will be self-supporting. £lOO has been invested
in the names of the trustees. During the three
months a great work has been done. The twelve
delegates have affiliated about as many counties,
and there are 150,00.0 labourers in union. In
several counties there are about 1,000 ; in others,
two or three thousand ; in Norfolk 20,000 in
union. There are few, if any counties, in which
the union has not been agitated at open-air
meetings. The result has been three strikes in
Warwickshire, one in Dorset, and one in
Worcestershire, and a lock-out in Oxfordshire, all
supported by the National Union. There have
been small lock-outs and strikes supported by the
branches. The invariable restili ha been the

811000,88 cf ttke 14bourers,in gainiug their terms, or
at any rate a satisfactory compromise. In some
cases, there being no settlement, the men have
migrated or emigrated. The wages have gone up at
least a shilling or two all over the country, and in
many cases there has been an advance of 48.
Farmers who last year paid £5 f)r the harvest
month, are now paying .£B. It is probable that
next summer 168. will be the ordinary standing
wages of farm labourers. The allotment
question has been discussed, but no definite action
taken. It is thought by the committee that there
is little use in memorializing landlords for garden
plots (as the West of England Labourers' Society)
is doing), and that it is preferable to agitate for
the franchise for the labourers, as with that
gained, the land question will soon be settled. It
was thought unnecessary to contradict a statement
that Mr. Arch was heading the insurrection of the
labourers of forty-four counties, with the view of
wresting the land from the aristocracy. The
labourers will be quite content with an acre or so,

LORD OEORGE HAMILTON, M.P., ON THE AORICUL.

At a cottager? flower and vegetable show held in
the Wilderness Park, Sevenoaks, the seat of C. H.

Mills, Esq., M.P., on Friday, Lord George
Hamilton, M.P., in distributing the prizes,
referred to the agricultural labourers' movement,
which had agitated that part of Kent for some
time post. He said that what he wished to point
out to the labourers was that if they were success-
ful in their combination throughout the country
three things must necessarily ensue. In the first
place, there would be a combination of the em-
ployers of labour; i° the second place, there could
not fail to be on the part of the employers a wish
to create additional facilities by which they oould
import labour from other parts of the country ;
and, thirdly, that if farmers found that they
experienced any difficulty in getting sufficient
labour, they would endeavour to minimise the
amount of manual labour • they required, and
would employ as much machinery as possible.
He did not doubt the right of any man to get al
much for his labour as ho could, but there were
two sides to every question. His own °portion
was that if one side asked with moderation that
would beget conciliation on the other, and he
would therefore especially urge oa all present,
employer as well as employed, that during the
next few months, should any difference arise, to
be as moderate and conciliatory as possible,
because concession on the one aide begot conces-
eion on the other. He would urge upon the
labourers not to indulge in agitation, althou4h he
admitted that in certain cases it • had resulted in
good, but as a rule to go straight t the employer,
and they might depend upon it that that would
receive a much more speedy response than if they
employed a mediator.

articles.title: PAST SESSION.
articles.text:
THE PAST SESSION.

Tun Session just closed has not been abso-
lutely idle, nor has its time been entirely
wasted. The Government succeeded in doing
some things, and in preventing others from
being done; whilst the Opposition did, and it
may also be said, prevented nothing. Mr.
GLADSTONE did not display any great degree
of pluck, whilst his rival was conspicuous
chiefly for his great prudence. The two great
Parliamentary chiefs seemed to have adopted
the policy of "let me alone and I'll let
you alone," or as has been sung of Admirals
BTNG and LA GALLISSONIERE—

We have lately been told
Of two admirals bold,
Who engaged in a terrible fight;
They met after noon,
Which I think was too soon,
_ .

As they both ran away before
The struggle, which from the flourishes made
outside the House promised to be determined
and fierce, was fought out with good-natured
smiles and gloved hands, and it finished
without a dangerous tapping of claret, or
discolouration of the " peepers " of either
gentleman.
So far so good, as regards the leaders of
our great political parties. In :regard to the
country, something has been done, but not a
great deal. The Ballot Bill has been carried
after a fifty years' fight, and even now by the
toleration of disgust and a sort of settled
belief that it must pass, rather than any
conviction as to its desirableness, It was
mutilated, and is limited as to duration, but it
will _hardly be allowed to lapse when its eight
years have expired, though, no doubt, every-
thing will be done in the meantime to make
it odious.. Still a point has been gained on
behalf of substantial reform, and Liberal men
will be grateful for it.
The Mines Regulation Bill is not what
it ought to be, nor we hope what it will
be. The responsibility of owners will
have to be more strictly defined by the
present Act, but for such an improvement
the miners must be content to wait. They
have got something, but not all, and therefore
must be prepared to fight again. The Public
Health Bill is not worth much, and the Licen-
sing Bill is just as likely to be a useless vexa-
tion as anything else. The Scotch Education
Bill has been pulled through, the religious
difficulty having been its great danger. The
damage intended by Mr. GORDON was re-
paired, but the words introduced by the
Lords into the preamble, like the slime
left on the snail's track, are offensive
rather than dangerous. The remission
of the twopence income tax is dile
rather to an overflowing exchequer than to
any generous impulse on the part of the
CHANCELLOR. Mr. HENRY Luau's Bill for
preventing corrupt practices at Munieipal
Elections may be the beginning of a very
necessary reform which the Government-mar
carry out next session. The Parks Bill only
shows an inclination to meddle and mar; and

behind much verbal rubbish there is visible a
disposition to abridge the freedom of public
assembly within these enclosures. A little
watchfulness and firmness on the part of the
people in London will, no doubt, preserve the
full right to hold public meetings without
vexatious intermeddling on the part of Mr.
AYIITON or his successors. Amongst other
things done and left undone may be noticed
the payment of Governor EYRE's expenses, an
act that may be regarded as an outrage on
justice. The shelving of all necessary law
reform, as much needed as any kind of re-
form practicable under the sun, but hopeless
of accomplishment so long as the nation looks
for it to our lawyers, is a great mistake.
The KEOGH business produced excitement, as
all feuds of bigotry usually do, but no good
can come from the decision of the Government
to prosecute the priests. Their influence will
be increased thereby, and substantial justice
rendered harder of attainment than ever.

Little has been done for which the working
people need be over thankful, but rectification
is within reach if working men, estimating the
value of sound legislation, set themselves
earnestly to work to improve the representa-
tion of the country by returning men to Par-
liament who have given thoughtful considera-
tion to the social and industrial question in
which they are specially interested.

THE BISHOP OF GLOUCESTER AND
BRISTOL.

IT is quite clear that Bishop ELLICOTI has
somewhere hidden in his sleeve a new gospel.
Men, in his eyes, are not all ot one blood, and
if they sympathise or seek to assist each
other across comaiy or parish boundaries
they are heretics, and ought to be held
anathe»ia maranatha. PETER had no business
at Joppa, and all that running about of the
Apostles was a mistake, which the Bishop of
GLOUCESTER would have rebuked, were he
living on his episcopal income at that time in
that neighbourhood. What business had PETER
at the "house of a tanner named SIMON, who
dwelt near the sea," only to set " class against
class," and make SIMON and the other
tanners, whose calling was regarded as almost
unclean, angry with those who so regarded it.
The Brsuor's letter to Mr. YEATs, taken
altogether, is a curious document, not only for
what it contains, but for what it omits. He
sticks to his statement as to the happy condi-
tion of mutual agreementbetween the labourers
and their employers. If one party lacks, the
other pours in its abundance, and the balance
is at once redressed. Pomp has taken physic
in the diocese of Gloucester and Bristol, and
this passage of the superflui to the needy
proves the justice of the heavens. The farmers
and landlords are even at this moment pre-
paring to " deal fairly" with their labourers.
When they have settled what fair dealing in
this matter of wages is, the BISHOP may
let the outside world know all about it, as
though on his own principle he should confine
the secret to his diocese. He might whisper
confidentially to a few of his brother bishops
that they may whisper it to landlords and
farmers elsewhere, that thus the blessing may
make glad the hearts of strange people living
in strange counties not within his episcopal
charge.

"It is wrong and utterly unjustifiable,"
says Bishop ELLicorr, "for strangers, who
can know.nothing of our local circumstances,
to come amongst us and to stir up dissension,
and set class against class." We really should
like to know whether the BISHOP really be-
lieves that people living outside his diocese
can know nothing of what is going on within.
Old Sir JOHN MA.UNDEVILLE, the early tra-
veller, speaks of a mysterious people who, in
times long past, were shut in by a mist, and
lived there without any soul being able to
penetrate the fog by which they are sur-
rounded. Those who listen may hear sounds
which indicate that the ordinary business of
life is going on, but nothing can be seen of
this strange and hidden race. tls this the ease
in the diocese of Gloucester and Bristol? Is
it a bidden. paradise? Do we simply hear
dreamy far-off sounds of the Bisuor's voice,
without any distinct understanding of what be
speaks about? Have our Royal Commissioners
penetrated there, inquired, and returned to the

outward world to tell us what they saw with
nothing but glamour in their eyes, as strangers
who could "know nothing" of the local cir-
cumstances of the place ?
For the future, it will be well if Gloucester
be made an exception in everything done for
the country generally by way of legislation,
or in any other way, seeing that people out-
side can know nothing about it. Are we
mistaken in supposing that England is in-
habited by Englishmen ? England, if the
Bisnor be an authority, is a lot of separate
counties, inhabited by people who cannot
possibly know anything of each other. Eleven
or twelve shillings a week as wages in certain
of these counties means something munificent
and princely. A stinking hovel means a rose-
embowered cot, and a smock-frock begrirneci
with clay, an embroidered robe, adding
dignity and grace to the wearer. That
they ought not "to send their Gloucestershire
men away to other counties" is very plain,
and for this benevolent statement the labourers
ought to hold the name of ELLIC6TT in eternal
reverence.

It is true in this letter to Mr. YEATES the
Bisnor made no allusion to the " horseponds,"
nor did he oiler any explanation of his sug-
gested duckings for agitators. Here again,
no doubt, the outside public is mistaken. A
horsepond in Gloucestershire is not like a vulgar
outside horsepond. It is a perfumed bath,
out of which those who are thrown in come
scented and made sweet, fit for the companion-
ship of the sleek and holy, who "pray
solemnly and earnestly" that things may go
right without being put right, or like
SAIMINAS' bath, fed by—
A thousand, petty rills
That tumble down tho snowy hills.
Possibly Bishop ELLICOTT is the fountains'
god, and his suggestion as to ducking agita-
tors was meant for their good.
Hold them gently till I fling
Water of this virtuous spring
On their temples, turn them twice
To the moonbeams ;. pinch them thrice.
That the labouring soul may draw the strength
of content, and be able to live happily in the
stench of an overcrowded hovel on eleven
shillings a week. Or the horsepond may be a
pool of Siloam, the waters of which make
whole the ailing.
Gloucester and its BISHOP are mysteries
which the British public should try to under-
stand. What are we to make of these words?
"This I solemnly declare, that during the
nine years I have been in this diocese, no
cases have ever been mentioned to me of
systematically unfair wages in any parish
that I have visited. And I certainly have
spoken freely with all classes, and have made
very free inquiries." We cannot distrust the
Bisnor. He cannot possibly be saying " the
thing which is not." But then how are we to
explain what wehave seen, what we know, what
everybody knows as to the condition of the
agricultural labour in England, not excluding
Gloucester? What does the Bauer regard
as " unfair " wages, or at what sum would he
consider fair wages? A definition of terms
would be of some use. Some few years back,
when education inquiries were made, above
one half of the. children in Gloucestershire,
between two and fifteen years, never entered
a school. The cottages in Gloucestershire are
now condemned as unfit for human habitations
by Her MAJESTY'S Commissioners. Wages
are about the same as in other agricultural
counties, and yet in tune years the BISHOP
heard no complaints. Perhaps the peasantry
find no profit in complaining ; perhaps the
Brsilor is too jolly a man to carry complaints
to ; perhaps they are afraid of the hersepond ;
perhaps—but why go on bothering one's brains
about the matter? Here the words of the
poet are absolutely true—

Thinking is a useless waste of thought,
And nought is everything, arid everything is
nought.

MR. MUNDELLA ON THE SESSION.

Mu. MUNDELL& is, as usual, the first to
give an account of his stewardship. It was
rendered in the most public form and place,
under the open sky, and in the largest space
within the borough which he represents.
Sheffield boasts of no building capable of hold-
ing such a gathering of its towusfolk as he
never fails to bring togeter.

On comparing the end of the session with
the beginning, this close observer finds the
Government strengthened by the interval.
The faults of the session of 1871 have been
in some measure retrieved, and the mis-
fortunes of the recess, which divided that
of 1872, have been succeeded by a happy
and merited success. The Opposition were
strong, lynx-eyed, and compact; but they
either lost or neglected opportunity. The
American Treaty, which at one moment
seemed hopelessly lost, was energetically
saved, and Mr. MUNDELLA. rejoices to think
that he was one to effect the rescue.
He is entitled to this comfort; and it may be
stated as a general truth, that none contribute
more essentially to preserve mutual confidence
between England and America than those
who, returning across the Atlantic to their
respective homes, come from inspiring confi-
dence in the minds of the strangers whom
they have visited, to assure their own
countrymen of the friendly feeling entertained
towards them by the best men on the other
side. "All thinking Christian men on both
sides of the Atlantic," observes Mr. MLIN-
DELLA, with great truth, " were anxious that
the difficulty should be amicably settled."
The consolidation in one of the whole Anglo-
Saxon influence spread so widely over the globe,
is, to all appearance, the best hope for man-
kind.

Mr. MTJNDELLA'S comparisons included one
between the Budgets of the last two years,
much to the advantage of the latter, as at once
unambitious, and, to a class between the poor
and the rich, alleviating. But, in five of the
measures which enjoy the distinction of a
separate paragraph in the Royal Message,
he finds that attribute of greatness which
dignifies a session. The Scotch are them-
selves the best judges of the Education Act
which applies to their country. The Licensing
Act is a compromise rather than a settlement.
The Public Health Act nobody will think of
regarding with unqualified approval until it has
been seen how the statute will work ; certainly
not, until the measure, now partial, has been
made complete. The Mines Regulation Act
comes nearest to the wishes of those who have
been long calling for it; and they will be
neither slow nor stinting in their acknow-
ledgments, if they find that it insuras better
protection and diminished risks.

The Ballot, however, is the one Act in
which all but the selfish have a com-
mon interest, and in the operation of
which a patriotic curiosity will exercise a
universal vigilance. What Mr. litsnmai
declared to be a corpse, has at at any rate
come to life again ; and it may be
expected that Mr. CHILDERS, on returning
from Pontefract, will give a good account of
its noiseless vitality. But, whatever may be
the case with the larger boroughs, the point to
be observed with most vigilance is the effect
that secret voting shall have upon the rela-
lations of land owners and land occupiers, with
reference to those matters as to which land-
lords and farmers may take different views of
their own interests and of each other's claims.
The agricultural labourer, too, has no small
stake in the experiment. If justice required
that the artizan should have a vote in the
borough, it equally requires that the peasant
should have one in the shire. In the mean-
time, the rent-receiver and the rent-payer will
have to settle it between themselves on which
of the two or in what proportions betwixt the
two the payment of living wages for the pro-
duction of the nation's food is to fall.

This is a review of the session devoid of
instructiveness to the working men. The
Government, without making much vaunt of
what they would do, or have done for them,
cannot be justly accused with total neglect
of their Claims and comfort. The Opposition,
who charged Ministers with such neglect,
hare neither Proved the accusation, nor en-
titled themselves to make it by superior atten-
tion of their own. We owe it, not to Mr.
GATLIOUNE lIIIIDY SO much as to Mr. AUSTIN
BItUCE, that the Mines Act is the fair and
promising law that it is. It was a good Bill,
declares Mr. MUNDELLA, when introduced
into the House. He never witnessed a better-
organized opposition to any measure than
among mineownera and their allies, In al-

most every instance, however, they defeated.
it. He had letters of thanks from the Millers'
Association for the part he took. One point
dealt with the hours of working for boys,
and the ages at which children should enter
the mine. It was proposed that boys should
go into the mine at 12 years of age, and
work 5-1 hours per week. The Opposition
tried to carry 112 hours in a fortnight, and
the Government, he was sorry to say, yielded
to that Opposition. He felt it incumbent to
stand up against both sides. He did so, got
a compact phalanx around him, and beat both
Government and Opposition. The miners said
he saved the Bill, as, without that clause,
it would have been worthless. In view of
the interested opposition which, through Tory
hypocrisy and official weakness, had, but for
Mr. MIINDELIA'S firmness and. energy, been
fatal to a good and beneficial measure, and
in view of the possibility of similar tactics
being had recourse to in future by the coin-
bination of similar interests, we see more and
more into the value and importance of the new
mode of voting, which not merely makes the
employed politically independent of his em-
ployer, but arms him with a moral weapon of
noiseless yet effectual defence.
It would be ungrateful towards Mr. MUN
DELLA to dismiss his review of the Session
without noticing his spontaneous efforts to
protect and benefit the working classes, and
his renewed pledges of devotion to the cause
of those from whose ranks, as he never con-
ceals, he himself emerged into wealth, station,
and importance. Ho brought in a Bill to
shorten the hours of children and young per-
sons in factories. Even Mr. DISRIELI professes
to believe that the moral and political strength
of a nation depends upon the preservation of
its physical health and vigour. Mr. M MID IMLI
acts upon that belief. While to up-grown men
it is being generally conceded that a week of
fifty-four hours labour is quite enough,
children of the tender ego of eleven are kept
for sixty hours in the silk mills. Anomalies
like this arc too gross to stand. The excellent
member has taken up the matter; and, by
GOD'S help, as he vows, he will not lay it down
until a just law of restriction is applicable to
all descriptions of labour by children and young
persons, whether in mine, factory, workshop,
and all other places of employment. We may be
sure that the hearty approval voted by his con-
stituents to his "eminently useful, indepen-
dent, and consistent course," will give him
fresh courage, energy, and zeal to persevere
in it to an honourable and, we trust, a pros-
perous end.

articles.title: WORKMEN AND SERVANTS' BILL.
articles.text:
WORKMEN AND SERVANTS' BILL.

ON Wednesday, Mr. HINDI i PALMER, 1110V8a
the second reading uf the "Workmen and
Servants (Compensation for Injuries) Bill."
He stated that the Bill was one of great
importance to the working classes, because, as
the law now stood, on judicial decision, work,.
men who sustained injuries in the course of
their employment, or (if they were killed by
the accident) their representatives were con-
stantly prevented from recovering damages
against their employers in oases where, if the
workman had been a third party as to whom
the relation of master and servant did not
exist, damages would clearly have been
obtained. A great injustice was thus occa-
sioned, which it was the object of the Bill to
remedy.

Mr. CHICHESTER FORTESCUE, on behalf of
the Government, said that he quite concurred
in the purpose of the Bill, and that he had
already prepared a Bill to embrace this
grievance with others, and that he hoped to
introduce it next session.

Upon this assurance, and considering the
period of the session, Mr. Pit.msta withdrew
the Bill. .

articles.title: TUE PEACE OF ,EUROPE THREATENED.
articles.text:
TUE PEACE OF
,EUROPE
THREATENED.

TIIE papers say that M. TIIIERS is disquieted
an iiabult
in consequence of the attitude assumed by
ttohe 113AUTU yLTAbNiII consequence of given
the French Ambassador at
Constantiuople. Emperors, Sultans, and
Kings are awkward customers to quarrel
with. BENEDETTI insulted the Knia of
PayserA, and we all know how dearly Franco

,10

• has paid for it. Some hundreds ef thousands
have been killed and wounded, many villages
burned, towns and cities bombarded, public
buildings destroyed, and private houses
plundered,'.bridges demolished, railways pulled.
up, and every other form of mischief the
"foul fiend." could suggest perpetrated. And
this, it must not be forgotten, for no more
sufficient reason than that two European
potentates and their agents bit their thumbs
at each other across the Rhine.
The cause of offence at Constantinople,
according to report, is not so grave as this.
It seems that the French Ambassador there,
whilst waiting for an audience, had the
audacity to sit down, because probably he
was fat and had. become fatigued by standing.
Etiquette was thus violated, and the honour
of the SULTAN wounded. This grave offence
having got into the hands of the diplomatists
has, as is usually the case, been bungled;
and now it would. appear that war by some
unlucky chance may arise from it. Thus,
because the French Ambassador was stout,
and during the hot weather became weary
and sat down at a wrong time and place,
armies may be called out, made to march
against each other, to load and fire, to stab
and slash, to wound, and kill, and burn, and
destroy, because a French Ambassador decided
to sit down when, according to rule, he ought
to have continued standing.
It would be instructive if somebody would
undertake to calculate how many wars in
Europe have arisen from like trivial causes;
how many lives have been destroyed in such
wars, and how much property plundered and
wasted.; how much of a money cost such
quarrels have been carried on at, and what
might have been done with this money for the
good of the various nations that have sacrificed
it if it had. been expended in peace and for
purposes of productive industry ; how many
roads and canals might be made, swamps
drained., factories built, distant regions ex-
plored, and all else done calculated to enrich
and elevate mankind. As a rule the churches
handle with great delicacy this vice of
sovereigns. They are prudent enough not to
run the risk of offending powerful friends.
It must be confessed, however, that in some
measure they make up for this by condeinning
with much vehemence the peccadilloes of the
poor,

Sometimes, however, in an indirect manner
the enormities of wars and the vices they
originate in, and which nearly always ac-
company them, are fittingly condemned.
When GULLIVER had related to the benevolent
KING of BROBDIGNAG With much vanity and
self-sufilcieney the wars and, other question.
able doings of Great Britain, that Monarch
said to him, "By what I have gathered from
your own relation, and the answers I have
with much pains winged and extorted from
you, I cannot but conclude the bulk of your
natives to be the most pernicious race of
little odious vermin that nature ever suffered
to crawl upon the surface of the earth." If
we limit the application of this to the war-like
sovereigns of the earth, it would be hazardous
to say that the description is not correct.
And if we have now another war because
an Ambassador's legs became tired and be
sat down when he was expected to be standing,
we shall have another illustration of its truth.
We shall understand more distinetly than
ever what "odious vermin" the kings of the
world are; and we shall, perhaps, see with
a little more clearness our own folly in
tolerating patiently such abominable vices as
monarchs indulge in at the public expense.
If we cannot see these things and compel
our kings to make the atrocities of war give
place to the activities of peace and the
humanising influences of industry, we had
better adopt the hideously grotesque customs
of Dahomey, and have our public carnivals,
festivals, and frolics on the spot where our
murders are committed, and in presence of
the horrors belonging to them.

articles.title: SOLDIERS LIA.RVESTING.
articles.text:
SOLDIERS LIA.RVESTING.

WE referred last week but one to the pro-
vision Mr. OkRDWELL is making for the
purpose of teaching trades to our soldiers,
under the pretext that they may be made
useful in providing by their labour for certain

wants in connection with the army. We did
this because we know how easily our autho-
rities can slide from what is correct and
legitimate to that which is neither the one
or the other, where the rights and interests of
working men are concerned. Having taught
soldiers to become efficient carpenters, brick-
layers, stonemasons, smiths, it is not in the
least unlikely that in case of a strike the
employing class might be enabled to avail
themselves of their labour coerce into sub-
mission unmanageable working men.
Does the following statement, which
appeared in the Daily News of Monday, throw
any light on this subject? "In consequence of
the representations of some of the farmers, the
authorities at Aldershot have arranged to send
a number of soldiers to assist in getting in the
harvest." We do not desire to construe this
too severely, but we should really like to know
the "ins and outs" of it. There are labourers'
strikes on now in many districts, and the
farmers can have the labour of the men if
they will pay them a living price for it, and
whatever else our army may be used for, it
must not be employed to prevent this. The
Leamington committee ought to have this
matter enquired into.

articles.title: HIGH PRICE OF MEAT.
articles.text:
THE HIGH PRICE OF MEAT.

WE have not seen a more apparently true
and intelligent account of the high price of
meat than that of a "Bedfordshire Farmer."
This gentleman, says, in substance, that agri-
culture has distinctive characteristics in diffe-
rent localities. Twenty or thirty years ago
it was exceptional if a farmer did not keep a
breeding flock, and wean some calves. For
years past it has been almost exceptional
where they have done so. Some parts of
England are better adapted for breeding than
others. In many turnip-growing and mutton-
producing districts, farmers bought the sheep
bred in Sussex, Wilts, Berks, and the western
counties. These arc put on to artificial food
to fat in the shortest time. This plan gene-
rally paid, and. produced abundant corn. The
supply from the counties named up to 1868
kept pretty ecinal to the demand, and mutton
was not too high. At that time good lambs
for winter feeding were at from 355. to 455.
each; now they cannot be bought under 555.
to 655. Shearling sheep were then bought
freely at from 455. to 25.;5 now it is difficult
to buy at all, and they cost from 60s. to 70s.
per head, is poor as may be, or about is. 21.
to is. 4d. per lb. In numberless instances
they are worth no more when fat than when
lean. The consequence is, that thousands of
acres which should and would have been under
turnips if sheep could be purchased .advanta-
geously to eat them, are now bare fallow, or
sown with a green crop, to plough in as a
manure, and thousands of acres of grow-
ing clover are also uneonsumecl for the same
reason. This state of things does not afford
much prospect of an early reduction in the
price of meat. The drought of 1868-1870
' compelled the large breeders to lessen, and in
many cases entirely to dispose of their flocks,
sold to be fatted the following year, or killed
as they were. The effect of these seasons,
coming so near to the cattle plague, was very
great, yet, in time, will cure itself; for breed-
ing is now more profitable than feeding, and
is therefore largely on the increase. The
change in the habits of the agricultural com-
munity conduces however to increase the price
of mutton and beef. Pork was almost the
only meat eaten by working men; now they
eat it very daintily, if at all, although generally
from is. to 2s. per stone lower in price. The
annually increasing consumption of veal and
lamb leads to the same result; but, for this,
the public, is to blame, not the butchers. They
are often obliged to give 10c1. per lb. for a
living sheep—and not unfrequently more. If
rind.erpest is again allowed to enter our herds,
we shall have to be vegetarians all.

articles.title: TUE NEWEST POPISLI MIRACLE.
articles.text:
TUE NEWEST POPISLI MIRACLE.

"Tan age of miracles is past," is one of
those sayings that come now and again to
everybody's lips. Whether true or not true,
it implies that an age of miracles has been.
We do not propose, however, in these columns,
to discuss either of these two questions. We
simply mean to compare a few ancient state-

ments with a very recent fact. In the second
book of the Jewish Kings, it is stated, that,
shortly after the death and burial of the
Prophet_ ELISTIA, the Moabites invaded the
land; that the invaders, surprised in the act
of burying a man killed in battle, cast him
into the sepulchre of EustrA ; and that, on the
man's body touching the bones of ELtsmt, he
recovered and stood upon his
,feet. In the
Gospel of MATTHEW, we are fold, that on one
of tha visits of JESUS CHRIST to the Lake of
Gennesaret, an that were diseased were
brought by their friends who besought him
that the sufferers might only touch the hem of
his garment, and that as many as touched were
made perfectly whole. In the Acts of the Apostles
again, we learn, that, when PAUL was at
Ephesus, GOD wrought special miracles through
him, so that from his body were brought unto
the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the
diseases departbd from them.

These are all the ancient statements which
it is necessary for our purpose to repeat. Let
them.now be compared with the very recent
facts communicated by the special correspon-
dent of the Daily News at Rome. In Tone
del Greco, a town at the foot of Vesuvius,
which has been repeatedly destroyed. by
volcanic eruptions and as frequently restored,
was born one Signor ROMANO, who in time
became Bishop of Ischia, a fine island in the
Bay of Naples. This Roman Catholic prelate
died; and, on the fifth of this month, was to
have been buried in his place of birth. Being
reported a saintly man, he was followed to the
grave in the public cemetery by a large crowd.
Before the gate had been passed, messengers
came hurrying from the town excitedly declar-
ing,that the dead body bad worked miracles. A
lame man had begun to walk, a second cripple
had thrown away his crutches, a mute had
spoken, and so forth. The air resounded with
cries of " Miracle ! miracle! miracle! The
bearers were compelled to retrace their steps
to the church from which they started. The
coffin and the corpse were replaced where they
had lain in state. Ilundreds of voices were
exclaiming, "Bring forth the sick, the
fevered, and the paralytic ! " The crucifix
was torn down from the altar, and the bishop's
corpse set up in its place. The episcopal
robes in which it had been arrayod were
stripped piecemeal from it, every one who
obtained the merest rag was persuaded that
he had received a wonder-working relic.

The priest of the church in which this
scene was enacted, came to find the corpse of
his bishop stripped perfectly naked, and the
building filled with a crowd excited to the
highest pitch. The tumult, indeed, was so
great that the reverend gentleman thought it
safer to retire than to stay. His entreaties
for order did but provoke anger, and he took
to his heels. Magistrate and Mayor had no
better success; and even when soldiers came
stratagem was found necessary in aid of
force. At this stage of the proceedings, the
steward, or manager of the church funds,
mounted the pulpit, and told the people that
the age of miracles was past. He might have
paid dearly for this unbelieving announce-
ment had not a sudden and violent ringing
of the bells diverted the attention of the
people and brought them out into the street
to ascertain the cause. The doors were
quickly shut and barred, the naked corpse
left to itself, and the military prevented a
renewal of the tumult.

Now, we are often told, and. sometimes
by leading statesmen of our own, that
the Jesuits have done an immense deal
for the eduoation of the people in all
quarters of the world. Here, then, is a
sample of the results. The town in which
this fanaticism was manifested, is not more
than two hours' ride from the city of Naples.
Its people have had all the benefits of
priestly tuition. What a pity that Prince
BISMARCK should deprive Ignorant Germany
of such supreme advantages. But no; the
Latins, no less than the Teutons, have had
quite enough of this sort of enlightenment.
The facts and scenes described occurred, not
merely where they did, but exactly one day
after the party of the priests had suffered, at
both Naples and Rome, a heavy blow and dis-
couragement, perhaps a fatal defeat, at the
hands of the ungrateful multitude on whom

they had in vain bestowed the ineffable aal

them implicit faith in such notions as that the

THE POSTMASTER-GENERAL VERSUS
THE POSTMEN.
ON the 31st day of July, 1872, the POST'
MASTER-GENERAL received a deputation of
London letter-carriers, who had been appointed
by their constituents to support a petition
signed by the whole of the London postmen.
which had been presented on March skh, sok'
hig for an immediate increase of pay, a higher
maximum rate of wages, and a better systeni
of promotion.
The POsTMASTER-GENERIL received them
with blandishments and compliments, inform..
ing them that a revised scale of wages which
had received the sanction of the LORDS OF TIES
TREASURY, would at once be acted upon, and
that—
He felt sure they would see that the question
of their position and pay had been very carefully
considered, and that he had shown no indisposition
to do what he could on their behalf consistently
with his duty to the public.
The public not being then in a position to
form a correct estimate of the advantages
gained by the postmen, and hearing one aids
of the question only, concluded that they had
been very fairly treated, and their ground of
complaint removed. Such, however, is not
the case, and on Thursday, the Bth inst., Mr.
H. EYEYN—
Asked the Postmaster-General if the Treasury
bad granted an increase of pay to those employed
in the minor establishment of the General Post
Office, and if so if he would state to the Houal
what is the amount, and how it has been distri-
buted, and whether a grant had been made to the
major establishment.
Mr. Monsen replied that the question of an in-
crease of pay to the minor establishment was noir
under the consideration of the Treasury. No
grant had been made to the Aft(for Establishment.
The answer given to Mr. El-11FX is most
conclusive, and it must be evident to the most
sceptical that the Post Office employes of the
minor establishment have not been fairly
treated, and that their grievances still remain
unredressed. The POSTMASTER-GENERAL, in
replying to the request for a better system of
promotion, said,
The rule under which a letter-carrier, on promo-
tion to be a sorter on his own application (without
loss of pay), was necessary for the good of the
service, and could not be departed from; exeept
at the risk of serious inconvenience. It was most
important that sorters should be taken as young
men and be in the prime of life, and this could bi
secured only by the present rule.
Then why did he not also explain bow it
was that most letter-carriers entered the
service with the distinct understanding, ap
published by their own official documents, that
if they conducted themselves properly they
had the opportunity of rising to .£3OP per
annum, and how is it that the department has
only just discovered that it would entail
serious inconvenience, and has so blasted tho
hopes and prospects of those who trusted i*
them?
The ground on which higher wages was asked
was the increase of cost in the necessaries of life.
This was a very large question. Higher pet,
because the coat of living was higher, could not
be confined to letter-carriers alone, atilt less to
letter-carriers in London; but meant a general
increase of remuneration throughout the Poet
Office, if not the whole Civil Service of the
country. It must be recollected, too, that argu-
manta in favour of raising wages on account of
temporary increase in the price of food, or the
labour market, applied with equal force in favour
of a reduction when prices fell or work was slack.
Admitted, and it might reasonably have been
urged, if allowed, that whereas the postman
would, owing to the increase, have to go short
of actual necessaries of life, Civil servants of
higher ranks in the public service must reduce
their social comforts, luxuries, &e. ; but, in
common justice and humanity, is it becoming
or politic of a wealthy country to merelY
allow the producers of a large proportion 01
that wealth a mere existence? But there is
still other reasons:why the wages of these men
should be increased. It should certainly be
an object of consideration to obtain the best
quality article in the market of labour, when
that labour is to be used and placed in positions
of trust and responsibility. There is sot the
slightest doubt but that many persons would
undertake to perform the duties of Controller,
Secretary, or even of Postmaster-Cieneral
himself, at a far less rate of remuneration than

the country at present pays for their services.
This is dangerous ground to tread upon, and
when a Cabinet Minister brings such argu-
ments to bear why his subordinates should
not be properly remunerated, it is time the
united trades of the country considered as to
the necessity of a Parliamentary inquiry,
with a view to the abolition of all sinecures,
and. the increase in. the wages of the real
workers of the establishment. The drones of
the hive must not devour all the honey to the
exclusion of the bees.

Mr. MONSELL, in his last Annual Report,
1810, says
Of the conduct of the officers during the past
year it is my duty no less than it is a pleasure
for me to speak in the highest possible terms, and
in saying this I wish it to be understood that I
refer not to individuals or the members of any
particular class or classes, but to all. All alike.
Those employed in the provincial as well as the
metropolitan offices seem to have been animated
by a single object—that of helping to prove, each
!within his own sphere of duty and to the extent of
his ability, that in undertaking the measures of
the year, various and extensive as they were, the
Post Office had not overate(' its power. It is this
spirit of zealous co-operation, which constitutes
the chief 'strength of the department, and gives it
confidence in the face of difficulties.

Now, if the POSTMAsTER-GENERAL is to
continue to report in this pleasing strain, he
must not recruit the army of Post Office labour
from the highways and byeways of the
country. Moral qualifications should also be
taken into account as well as physical fitness,
and this cannot be secured unless the pay
given be proportionate to the responsibility
incurred. In the above-named Report there
is no mention made of strikes of provincial
Post Office or Telegraph Employes, but we
presume that cannot be ignored in the next,
when it is to be hoped the total cost of sup-
pressing such will be enumerated and clearly
defined without it being necessary to bring the
subject before the House of Commons in the
ensuing session.
Arguments in favour of rising their wages when
prices rise, would equally apply when prices fell,
and work was slack.

The employes might well agree to this,
basing their argument ten or eleven years
back, when the present rate of pay Was
decided upon, and could also add that at that
time the net profit in 1661 (after payment of
all expenses) was only £603,717; with a total
cost of service of £3,161,141. Whereas the
net revenue (after payment of all expenses) in
1870 was £1,493, 610, with a total cost of
service of £3,435,865, or an increase of work-
ing expenses of £274,454, but with an
increase of profits in the corresponding period
of £989,893; and that the profits still con-
tinue to increase, and also that their work is
never slack.

It was, as they knew, the wish of' the depart-
ment that letter carriers should not work more
than eight hours a day or 48 hours in the week as
a rule; and when these hours were exceeded, and
the excess was likely to last, it was the business
of the proper officers to see that the work was
re-adjusted.

This is quite true, but how does a man fare
that dares to make such representation to the
"proper offieers ?" lie would at once, on
,some excuse or other, be taken off his walk,
and placed on one of the poorest that could be
selected in the district. This we can and will
prove through the columns of the BEE-HIVE,
should this statement be officially contra-
dicted, and if not so contradicted shall con-
clude that the assertions are correct. What-
ever the number of hours may be, it is in
many cases spread over 15 hours, and adding
the time it takes to come to and from their
homes, in many instances makes it between
16 and 17 hours. That their duties commence
lit the early hour of 5 a.m., summer and
ainter alike, while in most other branches of
skilled labour extra pay is allowed for all time
worked before 6 a.m., or after 5.30 p.m.

In stating their case the letter carriers referred
to wages only, but these do not adequately repre-
sent the value of a letter carrier's appointment.
The wages, as he had stated, began at 21s. a week,
rose by Is. a week to 255., and after 12 years'
service went on by is. a week to 30s. The
average wages were somewhat above 255., and
the majority of men in receipt of these wages were
only a little over 30 years of age. Letter carriers,
unlike skilled labourers, required to learn no trade,
and now they began to earn wages as telegraph
messengers as soon as they lett school. The
average wage.s, then, were 255. a week, and these
wages were not dependent on weather or fluctua-
tion in trade, but could be relied on week by week
through the year with absolute certainty. Besides
these wages a letter carrier had two suits of uniform
clothing yearly, the money value of which Could

not be put at less than is. 6d. a week. He had
medicine and attendance gratuitously when sick.
If laid up by ordinary sickness he received two-
thirds of his wages, and if hid up by an accident
while on duty he received full wages, and in either
case had no doctor's bill to pay.
An employs of the G.P.0., in a letter to us,
says, "We as a body fail to see these points in
the same light as Mr. MoNsELL. If we learn
no trade the department required of us a good
character dating almost from our birth, to-
gether with a bond of eighty pounds as a
security for our honesty, and we never have
earned anything as telegraph messengers. Other
men receive full wages (without any barrier)
on arriving at the period of manhood, viz :-
21 years of age; while about 30 years of
age is just the time when money is most
wanted to support a man struggling in the
battle of life to bring up a family of little ones
respectably, in most cases at that time all too
young to assist in their own support. It is
on this account we so earnestly desire to
see the "barrier " removed, the annual
increment increased, and the maximum
raised. This must be done, or we
shall (as we are, and for some time past have
been) sink lower and lower in social position.
This we are not prepared to do any longer;
an immediate increase on our present pay
must be granted, or the coining winter will to
us be a pitiable one, with coals, in all proba-
bility, at 2s. per hundred, and meat at famine
prices.

Again, he says we fully appreciate all these
benefits, but must at least maintain that they
were advanced on the sunny side of the ques-
tion, and to us appear to wear a very different
complexion. Few postmen sufficiently appre-
ciate the official medical doctor and his physic,
especially when the doctor is advised by the
inspector. Many men do belong to a club or
provident society.
Assistance that used to be afforded to a man
to insure his life has been for some time with.
drawn, and it would be interesting to us to
have a return of the number of ex-postmen
pensioners of £1 per week, and how long
the average life of such £1 pensioners is.
Then we are told there were the Christmas-
boxes, which he estimated at £lO 83. per
annum or 43. per week, but it might also be
said with absolute veracity that some few for-
tunate men receive £2O, and even more, but
that there are many that do not receive more
than one-fifth or one-eighth of that sum, and
in some cases even less. I have before me an
official order prohibiting me from soliciting
Christmas-boxes, while in the same order it
tells me that if I disagree with the other men
on the same walk as to their division or other-
wise, our superior officer will decide the dis-
pute, and the amount I may keep for myself.
A strange contradiction truly. Still these
Christmas-boxes are used as a reason for not
increasing our pay. It should also be remem-
bered that our Christmas-boxes do not come out
of the exchequer, whatever the amount may be,
but are an absolute present made us by the public
in return for credit for unpaid letters, wil-
lingness to oblige, &c., and would it not be
according to the law of equity if the Govern
m.ent pensioned us on all the etceteras, seeing
they do not ignore our right to them, as ad-
mitted by a Cabinet Minister
It was natural they should desire to better their
condition, but he did not think they made out
their case when they said they were unable to live
on their present wagei.

But he did not permit a reply. We, as a
body, are of a different opinion, and if, as is
probable, it does come to a few monster aggre-
gate outdoor meetings, our impression is that
Mr. MONSELL will be most unmiAtakeably
undeceived. We cannot live, in the proper
sense of the word, but do exist. " Stripes"
will not feed, clothe, and educate our
families, and whether "a small pecuniary
consideration" is given with them or not, we
would rather, as a body, receive them on our
backs as a punishment, than on our arms
as a reward. Suoh is the detestation in which
we hold the proposal to award them. With
every respect to that gentleman, we do affirm
that it would lead to the grossest abuses, be
injurious to ourselves, and detrimental to the
department. Of course none would receive
"stripe" unless they were favourably
reported of by their ' immediate =-
superior offioers; an we, at our small office,

should not hesitate long in pointing out who
are the favoured ones that would be recom-
mended or selected for the "honourable dis-
tinction." No stripes are needed for good
conduct in a department where the conduct
of all should be good, and to make an un-
enviable distinction of a few favoured ones
would be both impolitic and unjust. A power,
which wielded by a tyrannical inspector or
overseer, would be tremendous, because if he
had power to recommend the bestowal for
good conduct, he also should have power to
degrade by recommending their withdrawal,
and so degrading the recipient and on no con-
sideration whatever would the department be
justified in afterwards advancing him in the
service; and a very slight offence is quite
sufficient to offend some inspectors. "They are
, but human."

Would it not be a direct contradiotion of
the high eulogium passed on the service by
Mr. MONSELL himself, vide the report quoted
above, in which be most distinctly affirms
that the conduct of "all alike" was good.
Another strange contradiction, requiring ex-
planation.
He also said—

It was right to remind them that every letter
carrier was allowed fourteen days holiday in the
year.

This is not quite correct, although a very
pardonable error on his part, but unless the
two Sundays are counted as part of the work-
ing time, we make it but twelve; and as a
set-off against this, other bodies of workmen
have 52 Saturday half-holidays which they do
not, making in all 26 clear days to the
postmen's twelve.
It now only remains for the whole of
the employes of the nation to unite
in one energetic and universal effort. The
shackles of officialism must be unloosed and
all class distinction abolished, for once and for
ever, if success is to be obtained. In the
" bond of brotherhood" you're one. "United
you stand. Divided you fall." Therefore, we
say—Unite Unite! Unite! A "long pull,
a strong pull, and a pull altogether," and
victory will be yours. If money is required
let more hang back, but "let those give now
that ne'er subscribed before, those that sub-
scribed before now give the more." You must
succeed if you only have patience, and per-
severe. Hammer! Hammer ! Hammer
The nail must go home at last; therefore, we
say to the sorters, stompers, and letter-
carriers one and all, drive !it I—home !

articles.title: JOTTINGS OF A DEPUTATION TO LANCASHIRE.
articles.text:
JOTTINGS OF A DEPUTATION TO
LANCASHIRE.

Catching the 11.45 train, we leave the grand
Midland Terminus, after examining the superb
specimens of joiners' work which enclose the
various offices, ifro., criticising, however, the novel
but faulty intersection of mullions and chamfers
by which that intolerable objection—to the eye
of the London workman, viz,, showing the end
grain—is conspicuous.
But the train starts, and we are truly wafted
through the air by an express train. Somewhat
surprised to find ourselves travelling so fast at third
class fare, we refer to our tickets, and find the
words, "Govt. 3rd class" prominent, which at
once explains to us that we are in the act of
receiving the benefit of a Government interfer-
ence with the law of supply and demand, feeling
a sort of sympathy with the Government as
trades unionists. We relapse into a reverie as to
whether there is not something in trades union
principles after all that is worthy of imitation by
the governing powers of the country, seeing
moreover that the past action of the Government
in that direction has been, on all hands, acknow-
ledged to bs an unmixed blessing, to wit, the
Factory Acts, the Regulation of Coal Mines, and
other measures which have arbitrarily regulated
the employment of women and, children in factories
and mines.

At the end of oi hours we arrive at Manchester,
and arc received by the Secretary of the United
Trades, with a friendship .arid frankness which is
quite refreshing to us Londoners, with little time,
however, to do more than prepare ourselves AS best
we can for the meeting of carpenters and joiners
in the evening; after a walk round we arrive at
Brook-street, where a meeting is assembling to
receive the report of the deputation from London.
After a brief introduction, Messrs. the deputa-
tion find themselves face to fees with an intelligent
and appreciative audience. The circumstances,
however, are somewhat unfavourable for a first

debut at mblic speaking. The large square hall
is ill-adapted for sound, and extra exertion ii
necessary to make oneself heard, but our state-
ment being a plain and straightforward one, we
are easily understood, and soon succeed in enlis t
ing the sympathy of our audience.
Thorough men of business these Manchesto
folks. After the addresses of the deputation, and
without the slightest dictation or even a hint from
the platform as to their duty, a spontaneous pro-
position is made from the body of the meeting,
that the question be taken up at once, and
practical sympathy in the shape of a levy on the
trade is discussed, and without any difference of
opinion except as to the amount; after some dis-
cussion a levy of 6d. per week is adopted, and
after some routine business and mutual expres-
sions of regard in the shape of votes of thanks,
interspersed with a telling and actmewhat eulo-
gisticspeech from a well-known friend, the meeting
separates. Manchester men enjoy theadvantake of a
constant watchfulness over their interests by a
united committee of their trade, chosen in equal pro-
portion from the two large societies of this town.
Their duty is to see that all agreements between
employers and employed as to wages, working
rules, or what not, are properly observed and
enforced if necessary. It is to this committee We
are indebted for taking up the cause of the London
strike, and it is with them we retire to a private
room while they make the final arrangements for
collecting the money—at week end—using a
Lanky abbreviation.

The deputation is strongly urged by the com-
mittee to visit other towns in Lancashire before
returning to London. But being very restricted
in locomotive powers, an exchange of telegram}
and letters are necessary before the deputation
find themselves, through the kindness of a General
Secretary, introduced to the Secretary of a Branch
at Oldham. Arriving at Oldham, some prominent
characteristics of the place strike the mind at
once. Clatter, clatter, clatter, clatter. Along
every street clogs have either superseded shoes, or
taken precedence of them. Those appendages
which used to be known as bonnets, but which
have since degenerated into an endless variety of
indescribable head-gear, are totally absent here,
to-day at any rate ; one solitary instance,
apparently a fresh arrival from London,
stalks the street in all the plenitude of ele-
vated hair, &c., and in ludicrous contrast
to the unassuming, cleanly, and honest, looking
faces we meet at every step enclosed only by a
variety of neat kerchiefs fastened under the chin.
Millinery must be a bad business in Oldham, as
there is no attempt to bolster up a faulty face by
paltry artificial raanceuvres. But we arrive at
our destination, and although the front door is open,
we find no signs of life, and as there are no knockers
hero, we pass round to the backway, for
all houses have a backway in Lancashire.
We find our friend and his wife busily engaged
in horticulture, and on presenting our in-
troduction, although perfect strangers, we
are at once, familiarly speaking, at home,
so strong is the sense of a community of
Interests. Just a word about homes: it is a
charaoteristio of Englishmen that they can never
be severed entirely from home recollections. The
sentiment clings to them through life, and what-,
ever time may elapse, or distance separate them,
the old associations of home go with them, and
helps to mould their character imperceptibly per-
haps, but not the less surely. They afford, in
this respect, a striking contrast to many other
peoples—a very large class in America for in-
stance, and notably so in the case of a large por-
tion of French society, where the home sentiment,
if it exists at all, is of a most flimsy nature, and
certainly does not influence the national character.
Now at Oldham every working man has a separate
home of his own, not a home in the London senses
on the first, second, and third floor, but a house
to one's self and family, where you can breathe the
air -of local independence free from irksome
regulations and restraint. Although this
remark will apply to almost all towns in
Lancashire, it is especially noticeable in Oldham,
and the excellent influence it has upon the cha-
racter of the people is very marked. Sensible
people these of Oldham. They seem to have a
happy notion of adapting their habits to :their
means. There is no custom here of adjourning to
the publio to cheat the appetite on pay day.

A judgment has boon delivered by Mr. Serjeant
Wheeler, the judge of the Liverpool county court,
legalizing the detention of money by the agents
of a burial society, for the purpose of devoting
it to payment for masses for deceased members.
Upon the death of a woman named Ann Quirk,
who was a member of a Roman Cathalic burial
society, the ofliers of the society detained 10s. of
the funeral money for masses, and it was alleged
that it was properly withheld in accordance with
a rule of the society. On the part of the surviving
relatives of the deceased, it was urged that there
was no wish topave the masses said, and it was
admitted that this :wish was conveyed to the
oilicors of the society, who, however, refused to
respect it. His honour held that as the society was
a, CAI holic society, and there was a rule that a
portion of the funeral money was to be appropriated
fur masses, wbich rule must have been known to the
doe ~813 ii wh n he entered, the manager of the
Elociety was entitled to make the deduction.
