articles.title: FRIENDLY SOCIETY OF IRONFOUNDERS.
articles.text:
THE FRIENDLY SOCIETY OF IRON-
FOUNDERS.

The following is from this month's report :

"In laying before you the 217th monthly
report we are glad to say it is a good one. Trade
keeps excellent; nearly all our members are
employed; there is peace in all branches. As far
as the moulders are concerned, we have not a
single strike or lock-out in the trade; and yet, in
the face of all this, there appears signs of a
coming struggle. Coming events cast their shadows
before, and the atmosphere of trade and commerce
seems as heavily charged with thunder and 'light-
ning as the natural atmosphere in which we are
at present existing. Let us be prepared for it, so
that when it comes we shall not be found naked
and unprotected. Tho unprecedented high prices
of all the commodities of life cannot long exist as
they now are; there will be, by-and-bye, a terrific
collapse, and great will be the fall of those who
think their mountain is secure. For years the cry
has been that trades unions would drive the trade
out of the country, and this has been the ghost
that has haunted the minds of the class of men
who know little or nothing of trade societies, their
causes or results, amid which has been used by a
body of capitalists who are now doing more to
drive trade from the country than all the efforts
of all the trade societies since their commence-
ment. Labour has been struggling for ages to
have a fair share of that which it produces, but
every effort it makes capital tries to thwart, and
says, by its acts, "If you will not be content with
the pittance you are receiving, we will make the
need of your labour scarce, by enhancing the
price of the manufactured article to an unnatural
arid unwholesome figure." But rest assured,
brother members, that the evil results will recoil
upon those who bring them about. Haman was
hanged upon a gallows he himself caused to be
erected, and many a man has fallen into the pit
he dug for another. We never have, never will,
use threatening language ; but by the present
state of things we are forcibly reminded of a
passage in "Uncle Tom's Cabin." Two brothers
are in controversy on slavery; the one exclaims,
" We have our heel on the slave's neck, and we
will keep it there." " Yes," says the other, " like
an unwise engineer, sitting on the safety-valve of
hit boiler, until the steam assumes such a power as
to burst the boiler, when the whole are blown into
the air together." That sentiment has been veri-
fied in days gone by, in the history of many
countries; it may be so again. However, let us
be patient a little longer; 'tis true our shorter
hours and increased wages are not much benefit to
us at present, but they will be by-and-bye.
Things will find their level after awhile; let us be
prepared to retain the advantages we have already
gained, and they will help to hasten the time of
labour's reward. Get closer in unity; be ready
to assist each other in time of need; put shoulder
to shoulder, and when the crash comes, we shall
be like a solid square, into which the army of the
enemy will not be able to penetrate. But this
position will only be attained by means of con -
ciliation and forbearance with our employers. Lot
us render to all fair and honourable employers all
the help and aid we can, so as to enable them to
maintain their position. Give no countenance,
either by act or word, to the unscrupulous specu-
lator who is trying to build up a connection at the
expense of his fellow tradesman or his workman,
and by this moans wo shall establish for ourselves
a character for honesty of purpose and upright-
ness of action which will stand to us in tho time of
need better than even ill-gotten gold.

DANIEL GUILE.

articles.title: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT.
articles.text:
THE CRIMINAL LAW AMEND-
MENT ACT.

On Saturday afternoon a demonstration of the
various trades unions of Nottingham was held in
the New Cattle-market, in protestation against the
penal clauses of the Criminal Law Amendment
Act. There were previous processions of the
members of the different trades societies from their
respective meeting houses; and in a few instances
the processionists were preceded by bands of
music and placards bearing inscriptions which
denoted the purport of the demonstration.
The chair was occupied, as by previous arrange-
ment, by Mr. D. W. Heath, who introduced the
business, and read letters from the Hon. Auberon
Herbert, M.P., and Mr. A. J. Mundella, M.P.
The former thanked the committee fur their invi-
tation, and regretted his inability to accept it,
though he had desired to come and point out
where the present Act operated unjustly to the
workmen. The latter had wrote to say that he
fully sympathised with the object of the com-
mittee. He had done his utmost to prevent the
enactment in the first place, and secondly to
amend it.

Mr. Henry Aston said he had had placed in his
hand the following proposition, which he would
submit for approval :
That this meeting protests with indignation
against the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, 1872,
considering it one-sided and unjust, it being
especially directed against trade unionists ; that
we consider the severe penalties inflicted in several
instances for the so-called crime of picketing and
other constituted offences a monstrous injustice
and a violation of all just principles of civil
liberty; and this meeting of the working classes
of Nottingham pledge itself to use every legal
means to mitre the erasure of the Act from the
statute book, and calls upon Government and
Parliament to repeal the obnoxious measure with-
out delay.
Mr. Albert Richards seconded the motion.

Mr. D. Guile supported the resolution. He
believed, with their chairman, that the Act was
one-sided, unnecessary, and uncalled-for. It was
of no use tampering with anything like amenda-
tion, because in going in for amendment, they
admitted the necessity of the Bill: ergo, he
argued that their duty was not to try and amend
the measure, but to do what they could for its
repeal. Now, all that trades unionists required
was fair play, and this they were determined to
have, though it might be long before they
were enabled to get it. They should be deter-
mined that nothing should stand in their way.
Mr. Howell, who followed, also supported the
motion, and in doing so ho noticed seriatim the
several clauses of the Act. He had always main-
tained, and still maintained, that the common
law of the country was sufficient, and that there
was no necessity for the measure. Up to the end
of February 36 cases were said to have been tried,
and inLancashire several men had been imprisoned,
not for any offence against the person—not
for any molestation—but because they had been
standing in a public thoroughfare taking notice,
for the benefit of the union to which they belonged
of the number of men who were going in to supply
their places. For that simple act they were
adjudged to undergo three weeks' imprisonment
each. If they could not do all that had been
advocated by previous speakers in reference to
that Act, and that speedily, at least let them do
something to prevent honest, industrious, well-
conducted men from being thrown in a common
prison, as common felons, for doing that which
any other citizen had a right to do.
The motion was then carried unanimously, and
with acclamation.

Mr. Riley moved—
That this meeting further pledges itself at the
next Parliamentary election fur this borough to
support only such candidates as shall pledge them-
selves to vote for the total repeal of the Criminal
Law Amendment Act, 1871.
Mr. W. Hoe seconded the proposition.
The motion was unanimously carried.
Mr. West proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Guile
and Mr. Howell, the deputation.
The motion was seconded by Mr. Thornton, and
carried amidst loud applause.

tropolis shows, that in 1871 the quantity re-
ceived by water was 44,077 tons, while 72,386
tons came by rail. in 1848 the water supply
of fish to London reached 108,739 tons or
considerably more than double the quantity
received by way of the Thames last year.

articles.title: LATEST INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.
The King of Spain visited the public insti-
tutions of the town of Gijon, yesterday, and was
present at a banquet offered to him by the
Municipal Council, and in the evening he ap-
peared at the theatre. His Majesty was every-
where received enthusiastically.
Advices from Mexico state that the country
is tranquil, and that Porfirio Diaz, the leader
of the rebellion, has accepted the amnesty.
A Baby Show has been held in Dundeet at
which prizes were awarded for the heaviest
baby, the handsomest baby, and the best-
dressed baby. There were 46 competitors,
and the exhibition took place in the cattle
market.
The Liverpool magistrates have expressed
their intention to carry out at once the prO-
visions of the new Licensing Act. A meeting
was held yesterday to arrange the hours of
closing, and notices will be issued to publidana
and beersellers forthwith.

Some time ago the Corporation of Liverpool
decided to erect public baths in one of the
suburbs of the borough. It was estimated at
the time that the cost would be £ll,OOO ; but
such has been the increase in the cost of labour •
and materials that the work cannot now be
executed for less thanl.:l6,ooo. It has there-
fore been resolved to postpone the work.,
Mr. Kingdon, Q.C., will succeedl Mr.
Montagu Bere, Q.C., as Recorder of Bristol,
Mr. H. T. Cole, Q.C., having declined the ap-
pointment qualified with the proviso that the
new Recorder should cease to practise at the
Bristol Assizes.
John Hodgson Widdop, a draper, of Brad-
ford, was sentenced to six months' imprison-
ment by Baron Cleasby, at Leeds, on Wednes- -
day, for obtaining goods by false representations
within four months of the liquidation of his
affairs, by arrangement, under the Bankruptcy
Act.

Mr. Gladstone has intimated his intention
of forwarding to the Loan Museum of the
Dublin Exhibition an exquisitely designed
silver salver. Some important additions have
recently been made to the Sculpture Gallery,
including two very attractive marble groups
sent from Italy, and a. beautiful figure from
the studio of Mr. J. IL Foley, R.A.
As a consequence of the strike of the lamp-
lighters in Edinburgh, the lamps of the city
were on Tuesday allowed to burn all day.
The troops composing the Infantry Brigade
at Aldershot were exercised in field evolutions
on Wednesday, under the command of Gen.
Sir James Hope Grant.
The herring fishing north of the Tay has been
very successful during the last few days, while
south of the Firth the season's catch is much
under an average.
The "Galway Vindication Fund" closed on
Wednesday, the total subscriptions being up-
wards of £14,000. It is understood the entire
costs of the petition is about £12,000.
The judge of the Sheffield County Court
decided on Wednesday that a surgeon, not
being an apothecary, could not recover for
medicine supplied to his patients.
At the Leeds Assizes, yesterday, an account-
ant named Chambers, received £1,500 from
the Midland Railway Company, on account of
injuries received in a collision. Au applica-
lion to stay execution on the ground of
excessive damages was granted.
Another very bad case of fatal kicking,
this time from Warrington, came before Mr.
Justice Willes at the Liverpool assizes on
Wednesday. The prisoner convicted, John.
Loftus, was found guilty of manslaughter
only. The judge sentenced him to five years'
penal servitude. His lordship said he "feared
that unless the practice of kicking was put
down, it would bring some people to the
gallows." A similar sentence to that passed
on Loftus was the doom of a young woman who
had committed a heartless fraud on an aged
widow residing in Liverpool.

On Wednesday Princess Mary of Cambridge, .
less familiarly known under her wedded title
of Duchess of TEck, laid the foundation-stone
of some Church schools at Kingston-on-
Thames; the buildings, new and old, being
available for somo 700 children.

IL Thiors is stated to look " ten years
younger" than he did before he took his rest
at the sea-side.

John Doughty, a tramway conductor, was
discovered by detectives, employed to watch
him, to be systematically robbing his employ-
ers. So far as could be ascertained his pecU-
lations amounted to a considerable sum,. and
ho was sentenced to eighteen months' imprison-
ment with bard labour.

Mr. Scudamore reports that the total num-
ber of messages forwarded from postal tele-
graph stations in the United. Kingdom last
week was 320,555, being an increase of
68,057 oyer the corresponding period of last
year.

articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

At a meeting of the executive committee of
the Anti-Game Law League, held at 13,
Beaufort-buildings, on Monday last, it was de-
termined to issue an Anti-Ganze Law Circular
once a fortnight, in order to assist the agita-
tion which the League has commenced for the
abolition of the Game Laws.

M. Thiers is devoting a great part of his
time at Trouvillo to framing a proposal for
modifications in the Treaty, of Commerce
with England; and the President, after long
and close consultation with Count d'Harcourt,
the French 'Ambassador at London, feels con-
fident that the English Government will
accept his scheme.

After a visit to Trouville, for the purpose of
conferring with the President of the Republic
on the arrangements for the liberation of the
territory and on the approaching interview of
the three Emperors, M. Gontaut-Biron, the
French Ambassador at Berlin, has returned to
his post. Another French diplomatist has
quitted his post for good—Count Vogue, whose
leave of absence" from Constantinople is to
be permanent; he will probably be replaced by
Admiral Ronda° de Nourry.

Prussia, in the hours of her triumph, is
honouring the heroes of her humiliation and
resurrection. The other day a monument to
Stein was inaugurated; on Saturday it was
the turn of Frtedrioh Ludwig Jahn, more
familiarly known by his non do plume of
"Father John," who founded the societies for
athletic exercises that even England knows
as " Turnvereine," when a statue was un-
veiled to his honour.

A most useful example has been shown by
the justices lit Chesterfield Sessions,, who have
fined two miners somewhat heavilk for using
naked lights in Tapton Colliery, where safety
lamps should have been employed.

Railway rates, both for passengers and for
goods, are, in consequence of the enhanced
working expenses, to be raised generally from
the Ist of September. Such is announced to
be the decision arrived at by a meeting of
representatives of the leading lines, held the
other day in London.

Shoeburyness Artillery Camp was broken
lip after a competition for a prize offered by
the Association to the Royal Artillery for
home garrison service. Colonel Figher, Com-
mandant of the School of gunnery, afterwards
distributed the prizes, and made a telling and
practical speech to the men on the work they
had been doing and the way in which it had
been done, especially recommending a more
effectual method of shell practice at moving
objects. Colonel Chermside, commanding the
camp, has issued a most complimentary order
as to the behaviour of the men under very
trying circumstances of weather.

Brighton Aquarium was formally opened
in presence of a brilliant company—the Lord
Mayor of London, Mr. Sheriff Bennett, and
Dr. Carpenter, President of the British Asso-
ciation, being among those taking part in the
interesting ceremony. The Mayor of Brighton,
Mr. Burrows, congratulated the directors of
the Aquarium on their success, and declared
the place open; and Dr. Carpenter urged
that the Aquarium should be made a marine
observatory in the interests of science, and
thus should supply a want whioli had long
been experienced by naturalists in the study
of marine zoology. On behalf of the directors
it was promised that no exertion should be
wanting to make the establishment useful to
the scientific world.

Mr. Gladstone, Lord Ripon, and Mr. Bruce
have left town.

Lord Granard, who resigned the Lord-Lieu-
tenancy of Leitrim in consequence of his letter
on the Keogh judgment, has been succeeded
by Lord Southwell.

At Guildfora Assizes, damages of £25 were
given in favour of Mrs. Benson, who sued a
young man named Huntingdon for the seduc-
tion of her daughter, a girl of seventeen, under
circumstances peculiarly painful; Baron
Bramwell saying that if the facts given in
evidence were true, it was doubtful whether a
criminal inquiry should not have been made.

Before Mr. Mansfield, at Marylebone Police
-
court, a gentleman named Morice was charged
with publishing a "false and. defamatory
libel" with regard to Mr. Herbert Montagu
Sydney, who was accused of perjury in swear-
ing, at a former stage of the ease, that the
letter which contained the libel was in Mr.
Morice's hand-writing. The evidence in the
ease showed that the prosecutor and defendant
had been good friends until lately, but had
quarrelled; and in the end the charge was
withdrawn, Mr. Sydney's counsel accepting
the assurance of Mr. Morice that he did not
write the anonymous letter complained of.
The magistrate approved the arrangement be-
tween the partieli.

_
In an action for breach of promise of mar-
riage, tried at the Leeds Assmes on Monday,
a young lady named Packer, residing at Shef-
field, obtained £5OO damages against one Mr.
Skelton, a Suffolk farmer.

The Metropolitan magistrates continue to
teach occasional lessons of severity to those
who violently assault the police in the exeou-
Lion of their duty. For an offence of this
description one Edward Chepshaw, 40 years
of age, was on Monday sent to prison from
the Clerkenwell Police-court for six weeks,
with hard labour.

At the Highgate Police-court on Monday
Helen Millar was again examined on a charge
of having obtained money by false pretences
by means of a begging letter. The defence
was that the contents of the letter were true,
and as there was some doubt connected with
the case, the magistrates gave the prisoner
the benefit of it, and discharged her. At the
same time they expressed an opinion that
the Charity Organization Society had acted
rightly in having the matter investigated,

It appears to be the custom of many itine-
rant musicians upon the metropolitan lines of
railway to travel without paying their fares,
and they accomplish this by changing from
one platform to the other at the various
stations. One of this fraternity was on Mon-
day fined .£1 by the Hammersmith police
magistrate, and in default of payment he will
be imprisoned for fourteen days.

The Committee of Council on Education iii
England and in Scotland appeared in Tues-
day's Gazette. Earl Spencer is gazetted
Lord-Lieutenant of Northampton, and the
Rev. John Macleod Dean of the Order of the
Thistle.

We are informed in the report of the
Registrar-General that the cold weather which
set in on 30th ultimo continued throughout
last week, and the mean temperature of the
week at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich,
woe 59.2 deg., and 3 deg. below the average
for the corresponding period in 50 years.
More than an inch and a quarter of rain fell in
London half of which was measured on
Wednesday.

Last week the mortality in London and
twenty other large towns in the United King-
dom was at the rate of 23 deaths annually to
every 1,000 persons estimated to be living.
In the metropolis 2,169 births and 1,598 deaths
were registered, the former having been 27 and
the latter seventy below the average. Fifteen
persons died from small-pox, eighteen from
measles, 12 from scarlet fever, six from diph-
theria, 37 from whooping-cough, 22 from
different forms of fever (of which three were
certified as typhus, 12 as enteric: or typhoid,
and 7 as simple continued fever), and 441 from
diarrhcea. The fatal cases of each of these
diseases, except diarrhcoa, were considerably
below the corrected average numbers in the
corresponding week of the last ten years;
those of whooping-cough showed a consider-
able decline upon those returned in recent
weeks. So few deaths from small-pox have
not been returned in London in any week
since October, 1870.

Four murderers were executed on Tuesday
—three at Maidstone, viz., Francis Bradford.,
Thomas Moore, and James Tooth ; and one at
Stafford—Christopher Edwards.

Mr. Childers was recently waited upon by a
deputation anxious to bear his views on the
Permissive Bill. The right hon. gentleman
stated that personally he was not in favour of
the prohibition sought to be carried out by that
measure, and cited the disapprobation with
which last year's Licensing Bill was received
to show the impolioy of proposing sweeping
um.' organic chanqes before they had been
demanded by public opinion.

The last of the open pollings under the old
system was in the city of Aberdeen, and
resulted in the election of Mr, Fairley Leith,
and the last hustings was erected in the borough
of Wakefield on the occasion of the return of
Mr. W. S. Stanhope for the Southern Division
of the West Riding in succession to Lord
Milton.

A report has been received by the Local
Government Board from the Medical Officer of
the Privy Council, pointing out that by the
establishment of a direct and more rapidly-
traversed route between South Russia and
'
Persia the barriers which have hitherto stood
in the
way of the importation of Asiatic
cholera into Europe are seriously diminished.

Richard. Johnstone, a solicitor, was corn-
inited for trial at Dublin for having fired at
an I wounded a labourer, named Kearns, in
tin Pboanix Park last April.

A rumour has reached the Dublin Mail that
it is in contemplation to transfer the whole of
the Account Department of the Irish Pest
Ofßoo to London.

Invited to a dinner at the Ga,rriek Club, Mr
Stanley, the discover of Livingstone, detailed
his famous journey into Central Africa, and
described minutely the condition in which he
found the great English traveller.

His Excellency Prince Terashima and nine
other Japanese having arrived in Liverpool by
the China, and arrangements having been
made to receive the remaining forty members
of the mission, who are expected to come in
the Olympus, Earl Granville has presented the
Japanese Envoy to her Majesty the Queen. at
Osborne. Prince Terashitna, on his part,
handed in his credentials as the representative
of Mikado.

Already the troops destined to take part in
the autumn manceuvres are moving upon
Blandford by road and rail. Standing orders
have been issued detailing camp and field
duties, and giving specific directions to both
officers and men in relation to baggage, provi-
sions, and general conduct.

Cardinal Antonelli has had a violent dis-
cussion with the Pope, in the course of which
the Cardinal declared that he could not re-
main in ()taw unless his Holiness treated with
the Italian Government. Cardinal Auto-
nelli has, it is said, requested the clerical
journals to abstain from publishing the Pope's
speeches.

On Tuesday, while in Paris, M. Thiers pre-
sided at a Council of Ministers, gave a fare-
well audience to Djemil Podia, the Turkish
Ambassador, who is about to return to Con-
stantinople, and had an interview with Lord
Lyons on the subject, it is believed, of the
French Treaty of Commerce.

It is stated bythe Paris Liberte, that Father
Hyacinthe and the Abbe' Michaud, late vicar
of the Madeleine, propose to go to New Cale-
donia to establish a Church, in accordance
with their own doctrines, among the political
convicts of that penal settlement.

The Mediterranean fleet, consisting of five
ironolads, under the command of Vice-Ad-
miral Yelverton, has arrived at Coruna&

There has been a collision in the Hooglily
between the Khedive, one of the Peninsular
and Oriental Company's vessels, and another
steamer named the Aral. No damage was done
to the former, but the latter sank.

The Southwark police magistrate was
engaged for genie time on Tuesday in investi-
gating a charge of disorderly conduct, and
assaulting the police, against two men named
Phipps and Riley, who were defended by the
Labour Protection League. The defendants,
with a number of other men, were out on
strike, and because some of their fellow work-
men declined to turn out, Phipps and Riley
resorted to menaces and molestation. It was
while they were pursuing this course of
conduct that the offence was committed with
which they were charged. Each of them was
fined £lO, which was paid.

A. boiler blew up on the promises of a steam
saw-mill proprietor in Whitechapel a few days
ago. The stoker was killed, and several other
persons were wore or leas injured.

On Monday the capital sentence was carried
out upon Charles Holmes, a labourer, within
the walls of Worcester county prison. He had
been sentenced to death for the murder of his
wife at Bromsgrove.

Another Communist has been condemned to
death by a French Court-martial. Ile was
arrested more than a year since' but was set
at liberty then for want of proof. Some few
months ago he was again arrested, and he has
now been convicted. One of the charges
brought against him was that of pillaging and
setting tire to the Palace of the Legion of
Honour.

A fire broke out early. on Wednesday morn-
ing at a large cotton factory at Geneva, and
spread with such rapidity that, owing to the
scarcity of water, nothing could be done to
stop the progress of the flames, and in about
an hour the whole of the premises were
destroyed. The loss is estimated at £400,000.
Eight hundred workmen are thrown out of
employment by this terrible calamity,

According to a letter from Rome in the
Perseveranza of Milan, the Pope has written
a letter to M. Thiers, warmly congratulating
him on the success of the great French Loan.

The Brighton Meeting of the British Asso-
ciation was opened on Wednesday. The in-
augural address was delivered by Professor
Carpenter, Registrar of the University of Lon-
don, who disousssed at seine length the con-
sideration of the mental processes by which
are formed those fundamental conceptions of
matter and force, of cause and effect, of law
and order, which furnish the basis of all
scientifie reasoning, and constitute the Philo-
sophia prima 9f Bacon,

is

Lima has witnessed a "smart little thing"
in revolutions. The President, Balta, has been
assassinatd by Guitterez, leader of a revolu-
tionary movement, who proclaimed himself
Dictator—and was hanged by the people to a
lamp-post,

The inquest held on the body of James
Flynn the condemned man, who starved
himself to death in Manchester Gaol, evinces
an extraordinary amount of determination on.
the part of the prisoner. It appears that
after a pint of gruelly broth had been injected
into his mouth by means of a stomach pump,
Flynn placed his fingers into his mouth, and
vomited the food. The jury returned a verdict
of death from exhaustion, caused by wilful
abstinence from food.

Lending a ring to a conjuror was the origin
of a dispute which, in the end, came before
the magistrate at Marlborough-street Police-
court for decision. Mrs. Hannah aslaney, at
present not living with her husband, stated
that, being in a house in Panton-street where
the defendant, M. Martini, was conjuring, she
lent him a diamond ring, value £l4 10s. On
leaving she forgot the jewel, and, on going
back, was offered a ring which was not hers.
On the part of Martini, it was stated that a
"ring trick" had been performed, but that
the ring had not been changed. Mr. Newton,
however, ordered the defendant to pay £l4 10s.
and costs, or go to prison for a month.

At 6 per cent. annual interest the Govern-
ment of Spain has obtained a loan of 25
millions of reale from the Bank of that coun-
try. As a guarantee for the repayment of that
sum, the Ministry is reported to have allotted
the income resulting from several taxes.

A "large-sized, old, and artful " monkey
was the subject of complaint at Greenwich
Police-court. It was stated by a gentleman
that the animal had slipped its chain and
pursued the applicant's wife with such persis
tenoy that she had to jump over a fence to
avoid it Mr. Maude, remarking that he had
neither the power to apprehend the monkey
nor to issue a Chancery injunction against its
owner, referred the complainant to a
_civil
court for a remedy.

In hope of finding ber husband, Mrs.
Mary Ann Eagle, the wife of a confectioner in
the Edgware-road, made application to Mr.
D'Eyncourt, at the Marylobelia Police-court.
It appeared that Mr. Eagle, Who is a vestry
man of Marylebone, had been for some time
ailing, and when ke loft home on Thursday
morning was suffering from violent pains in
the head. He had not since returned; and as
all his accounts, both as regarded his own
business and that of a loan society, of which
he was secretary, were correct, it was diffi-
cult to assign any reason for his absence.

Mendez and Trevino, the insurgent chiefs,
and two other important rebel leaders, having
accepted the amnesty offered to political
offenders in Mexico, peace and quiet are pro
-
dieted for the future. Meanwhile the export
of silver is very considerable; and two mil-
lion dollars, it is said, will be sent from Vera
Cruz to Europe about the end of this month.

At the half-yearly meeting of the Great
Eastern Railway shareholders a sum of
£2,000 was voted to be expended on a piece of
plate, for presentation to the Marquis of Salis-
bury, for his services as Chairman of the
Board during four years. A significant state-
ment was made by Mr. Lightly Simpson the
present chairman, viz., that the directors arc
negotiating for the purchase of Belgian coal
for both steamers and railroads.

At the Clerkenwell Police-court Lydia
Venables, 26 years of age has been charged
witli having murdered her child Eliza by
cutting her throat with a table knife. The
prisoner, a widow, had been living with a
cabman as his wife for the past sixteen months,
and it was to unhappiness in her domestic life
that the perpetration of the crime was attri-
buted. She was committed for trial

A conductor in the employment of the
North Metropolitan Tramway Company has
been convicted at the Middlesex Sessions of
embezzlement, and sentenced to be imprisoned
and kept to hard labour for eighteen calendar
months.

In accordance with ancient custom the
Derry Apprentice Buys celebrated the anni-
versary of the relief of the city with a pro-
cessional visit to the cathedral. After service,
they made a circuit of the city, accompanied
by bands and, bannereta ; and, the Catholics
being conspicuous only by their absence, no
serious disturbance took place. Although
the city is at present "proclaimed," cannon.
were fired in honour of the occasion, and the
proceedings closed at night with a banquet.

Mr. Muni()lla addressed an open-air meeting
at Sheffield, and, reviewing the events of the
past session, warmly praised, the =het of
Government.

Israel Moss, being troubled with a son who
was given to steeling and "neglecting his
prayers," chastised him with a broomstick,
and for doing so was indicted at Worship
street Poliee-court. Evidence given showed
that the lad was well-nigh incorrigible,
whereupon Mr. llushby, remarking that he
did not think it right to interfere between
father and son, discharged the defendant.

A violent assault having been committed by
a soldier of the Coldstream Guards upon two
women, a curious question of identity arose at
Westminster Police-court. The man in cus-
tody, James Moore, had previously owned to
committing the outrage, when a comrade,
named Smith, came foi ward, and asserted that
it was he who had struck the complainants.
Mr. Woolrych, however, committed Moose for
trial.

By the French-press the meeting of the
three Emperors at Berlin is regarded with
considerable distrust, and the Temps states
that the object of Prince Bismarck is to form
a league between Germany, Austria, and
Rnssia which shall isolate France, and render
revenge on her part impossible.

James Flynn, who was sentenced to death
at the late South Lancashire assizes, died on.
Tuesday from exhaustion, having aystemati,
cally refused to partake of any food since his
condemnation.

In a case heard on Tuesday at the Middle-
sex Sessions, a lodging-house keeper of
George-street, Shoreditoh, stated that in her
three bedrooms she accommodated 92 persons
of both sexes, who paid her threepence each
for their beds.

At the Marylebone Pollee-oourt on Tuesday
a powerful fellow, Charles Cooper by n ame,
was sentenced to three months' imprisonment
for a violent assault upon the police. At
Greenwich, a bricklayer was sent to prison
for two months for a similar offence.

The charge against a respectably-dressed
young woman, named Harriet Chapman, of
having obtained money by false pretences,
was further investigated at Wandsworth
Police-court on Tuesday. The prisoner had
solicited subscript;ons to take for a day in
the country a number of pauper children, and
had represented herself to be the matron of
the workhouse. She was sentenced to fourteen
days' imprisonment.

• A cattle dealer of Doneaster' named Rob-
son, was on Tuesday sentenced to five years'
penal servitude at the Leeds Assizes, for
having attempted to obtain money, by false
pretences from the Manchester Sheffield and
Lincolnshire Railway Company by falsely
ewearing that he had been injured in a colli-
sion.

A butcher residing at Bootle, named Robert
Smith, was discovered selling the flesh of a pig
which had died from scarlatina. lie was fined
46 and Li 17s. costs.

At Lambeth Police Court Maria Mitchell,
who is described as a "determined-looking
woman," was charged with committing a
murderous assault upon Thomas Berry with
whom she lived as his wife. Roused to
jealousy by Berry, who bad " treated " a
former landlady, she knocked him down with
a bottle, and then seizing a paraffin lamp
poured the contents over him, and set him on
fire. Ile was severely burned, as well as
beaten, and the magistrate, who thought it a
very serious case, remanded the prisoner.

Princess Christian, just now residing at
Cumberland Lodge, Windsor, has given birth
to a daughter. Her Royal Highness and the
infant Princess are both doing well.

In view of the approaching 4th of Septem-
ber, a circular has been issued to all the Con-
reils-Generanx and Prefects enjoining absten-
tion from political manifestations.

Two immense turtles are nmong the latest
arrivals at the Brighton aquarium.

Amongst others who have given in their
adherence to the Greeley party is Andrew
Johnsonf the ex-President to the United
Sudo.

Cape mails bring from the diamond fields
news of a, robbery of £50,000 worth of dia-
monds, from the post-bags at De Beer's New
Rush. A man named Harding was captured
on board a ship_ at the Cape, on suspicion of
being concerned in the robbery, and a double-
barrelled gun belonging to him was found to
be ()barged with 1,067 'Vaal diamonds. 1,200
more of the precious stones were found about
his clothing, besides money to a considerable
amount.

articles.text:
THE VitORXINO MAN'S PLATFORM.

To the Editor of the "BEE-Ilivz."

Pall Mall Gazette of Thursday
last oontains the following :—" The Post states '
that a meeting was held last evening at the
Arundel Club to consider the propositions
which have been put forward by Mr. Samuel
Morley, M. P. The meeting was strictly
private, none being admitted save the dele-
gates of political societies. Each society
numbering 100 members or upwards, was per-
mitted to send two delegates, one delegate
only being admitted from a society consisting
of less than 100 members. The meeting was
one of working men only, Mr. Morley not
being present.'
So at last the truth is out. Mr. Morley, the
chairman and originator of the Cannon-street
Hotel meeting for the avowed and ostensible
purpose Of suggesting to the working class the
line of policy they should adopt at the next
general election, has submitted the proposi-
tions to a hole-and-oorner meeting, at which
no one was admitted "save the delegates of
political societies i." and considering that Mr.
Morley is a thick-and-thin supporter of Mr.
Gladstone, I am justified in assuming that he
addressed such propositions to Mr. Gladstonee's
supporters alone.
Now I submit that those propositions ought
to have been addressed to the working class
in your columns, the BsE-HrvE being their
recognised organ, and in your columns Mr.
Morley's propositions would assuredly have
received that just criticism of which no honest
man need be afraid; but, as it now appears
that Mr. Morley's is a political movement to
induce the working class to support Mr. Glad-
stone, he was wise in his generation.

But I accept this conduct of Mr. Morley's
as an admission that he believes his proposi-
tions will not bear any comparison with the
suggestion which I have made in your
columns, regard being only bad to that which
is best for the interest of the working class to
adopt, and just in proportion as he succeeds
in keeping those propositions secret will he
prove that he knows he has acted wrong in
pretending that he was seeking the benefit of
the working class alone.—Yours, &e.
RIGBY
Aug. 12, 1871.

THE DISITT.E IN THE LONDON
BUILDING TRADE.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Sin,—l have read the correspondence in
your excellent and increasingly valuable paper.
between Mr. Mitchley and Mr. Broadhurst,
and think that Mr. Mitchloy in his last letter
evinces a degree of animus not at all credit-
able to a trades unionist. It is much to be
preferred that in those discussions upon their
internal affairs, conducted through the medium
of the public press, trades unionists generally
should confine themselves to statements of
fad, and arguments based thereon, and en-
deavour to avoid entirely those personal recri-
minations which have been too often the dis-
grace of nearly every club-room in the king-
dom. In reference to the present and recent,
so far as the masons are concerned, dispute in
the building trade in London, permit me to
say, from a very considerable official experi-
ence in connection with the working of a
trade union, that the one great evil which
so often results in the complete defeat
of labour in the creatien of a multitude
of oppositionists and consequent demoraliza-
tion of trade societies, is that, of a.ppointin9l
delegates to meet employers with their, hands
completely tied behind their backs. Nothing
can be more ridiculous or unworthy a sensible
body of men than that of appointing negotia-
tors without any power .to negotiate. So
far as we, in these relater parts of the
country, are able to understand the attitude
of the London masons, we believe that they
have done a wise thing; they have broken
through a stupid custom, and prudently, drawn
up a moderate and reasonable memorial, and
appointed delegates to wait upon the employ-
ers, empowered to "negotiate discretionally ; '
and of course such power implies the willing-
ness to accept a compromise if all they desired
could not be obtained. In the negotiation, if
the masons did not obtain the best half of the
advantage they certainly obtained solid and
substantial gain, quite sufficient to recommend
for further trial the principle of "discretionary
negotiation."_

It is no isolated opinion that one very con-
siderable branch of the building trade showed
the existenoe amongst themselves of a spirit of
paltry jealousy and foolish conceit when they
determined to exclude from their private
councils some of their most enlightened and
experienced members, such as Mr: Applegarth,
and that for no reason that sensible men oan
admit as valid. But for such an unwise reso-
lution possible, the dispute might weeks
ago have been satisfactorily adjusted.--I am,
Sir, yours truly,

W:ir. GRAMM
